verseByVerse.commentary:
let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead — by him this man is standing before you well. This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone.

By the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead. The answer to their question, and the gospel in one sentence. You crucified him; God raised him.

By him this man is standing before you well. The healed man is standing there (v. 14). The proof is visible.

This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone. Key words. From Psalm 118:22, which Jesus applied to himself after the parable of the tenants (Luke 20:17), with these same leaders listening. The builders, Israel’s leaders, rejected the stone; God made it the cornerstone, the foundation stone that holds the building together. Jesus is the foundation of the new temple, the church (1 Peter 2:4–8; Ephesians 2:20).

In a sentence. Peter told them and all Israel that this man stood healed by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom they crucified and God raised, the stone the builders rejected that has become the cornerstone.

For worship. The stone they rejected holds up everything. Build your life on him.

parallels.desc: the stone the builders rejected

verseByVerse.quote: "And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.

And there is salvation in no one else. Key words. Peter moves from the healing to salvation itself. Not only was this man healed by Jesus alone; all salvation is in Jesus alone.

For there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved. “No other name”: no other person, no other way. “Under heaven”: anywhere in the world. “Given”: by God. “Must”: it is God’s appointed way, and it is necessary. This is the exclusive claim of the gospel, spoken to the highest religious court of the only nation that knew the true God.

Where Christians differ: are there other ways of salvation? Pluralists hold that all religions lead to God; inclusivists that people may be saved by Christ through other religions, without knowing him. Verdict: “no other name” is unmistakable. Even Israel’s religion, without Christ, could not save. Salvation is found in Jesus alone, through faith in him (John 14:6; 1 Timothy 2:5). This is why the gospel must be preached to every nation (Romans 10:13–15). It is said not with arrogance, but with urgency and love.

In a sentence. There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to people by which we must be saved.

For worship. One name saves. Make it known, because there is no other.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus. But seeing the man who was healed standing beside them, they had nothing to say in opposition.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus. But seeing the man who was healed standing beside them, they had nothing to say in opposition.

When they saw the boldness of Peter and John. Key words. “Boldness” (parrēsian): freedom of speech, frankness, confidence. A key word in Acts (vv. 29, 31; 28:31). It is the Spirit’s gift.

And perceived that they were uneducated, common men. “Uneducated, common men” means they had no formal training in the rabbinic schools, not that they were illiterate. “Common” (idiōtai): laymen, ordinary people. Galilean fishermen arguing from Scripture with the scholars of Israel.

And they recognized that they had been with Jesus. Key words. The explanation. Jesus too had astonished them without formal training (John 7:15). Time with Jesus made them what they were. Character and confidence like his.

But seeing the man who was healed standing beside them, they had nothing to say in opposition. You can’t argue with a walking man.

In a sentence. The council was astonished at the boldness of Peter and John, seeing that they were ordinary men without training, and recognised that they had been with Jesus, and with the healed man standing there, they could say nothing against it.

On a Tuesday. Spend time with Jesus. People will notice.
verseByVerse.note: “Uneducated, common men” means they had no formal training in the law under a rabbi — not that they were illiterate.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they had commanded them to leave the council, they conferred with one another, saying, "What shall we do with these men? For that a notable sign has been performed through them is evident to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when they had commanded them to leave the council, they conferred with one another, saying, “What shall we do with these men? For that a notable sign has been performed through them is evident to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it.

They conferred with one another. A private discussion. How did Luke know? Perhaps through a sympathetic member, such as Gamaliel, Nicodemus or Joseph of Arimathea, or Paul, a later insider.

What shall we do with these men? The same helpless question they asked about Jesus (John 11:47).

For that a notable sign has been performed through them is evident to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it. Key words. An admission from the enemies of the gospel. They do not deny the miracle. They cannot. Their problem is not evidence, but unwillingness.

In a sentence. After sending them out, the council discussed what to do with them, since all Jerusalem knew they had performed a notable sign that could not be denied.

For worship. The evidence for Christ is there, even his enemies admit it. Unbelief is a matter of the will.

verseByVerse.quote: "But in order that it may spread no further among the people, let us warn them to speak no more to anyone in this name." So they called them and charged them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But in order that it may spread no further among the people, let us warn them to speak no more to anyone in this name. So they called them and charged them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus.

In order that it may spread no further among the people. Damage control. They want to stop the spread.

Let us warn them to speak no more to anyone in this name. They won’t even say the name Jesus.

So they called them and charged them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. A direct order from the highest religious authority in Israel. The first ban on evangelism. Many have followed.

In a sentence. To stop it spreading, they decided to warn them, and called them in and ordered them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus.

On a Tuesday. The world often says, “Believe what you like, but don’t speak in Jesus’ name.” Be ready for that pressure.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter and John answered them, "Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge, for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter and John answered them, “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge, for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard.”

Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge. Key words. A respectful but firm refusal. They appeal to a higher court. Human authority is real and must normally be obeyed (Romans 13:1–7). But when it commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, we must obey God (5:29).

For we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard. “Cannot”: they are compelled, as Jeremiah was (Jeremiah 20:9), and Paul (1 Corinthians 9:16). Eyewitnesses can’t unsee what they saw.

Where Christians differ: civil disobedience. Some say Christians must always obey the government; others that they may resist any unjust law. Verdict: Christians are to submit to governing authorities and pray for them (1 Timothy 2:1–2), honouring even unjust rulers (1 Peter 2:13–17). But where the state commands sin or forbids obedience to God, as in forbidding the gospel, we must obey God, openly, peacefully, and accept the consequences, as the apostles did. This is not rebellion but faithfulness.

In a sentence. Peter and John answered that the council must judge whether it was right before God to listen to them rather than to God, for they could not stop speaking about what they had seen and heard.

For worship. When you must choose between God and men, choose God. Gently, respectfully, firmly.

parallels.desc: we must obey God rather than men

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had further threatened them, they let them go, finding no way to punish them, because of the people, for all were praising God for what had happened. For the man on whom this sign of healing was performed was more than forty years old.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they had further threatened them, they let them go, finding no way to punish them, because of the people, for all were praising God for what had happened. For the man on whom this sign of healing was performed was more than forty years old.

And when they had further threatened them, they let them go. Threats, but no punishment. Yet.

Finding no way to punish them, because of the people, for all were praising God. Public opinion protected them, as it had protected Jesus for a time (Luke 20:19; 22:2).

For the man on whom this sign of healing was performed was more than forty years old. Lame for over forty years. Everyone knew him. The healing was undeniable. Luke the doctor notes the age.

In a sentence. After further threats, they let them go, finding no way to punish them because the people were praising God, for the healed man was over forty.

For worship. God can use even public opinion to protect his servants. He rules over all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–37 — Prayer, Power, and the Community of Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Released, Peter and John went back to their own people and reported what the chief priests and elders had said. Hearing it, the believers prayed together to the sovereign Lord, maker of heaven, earth, sea and everything in them. They recalled that the Holy Spirit had spoken through David, asking why the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain, why kings and rulers band together against the Lord and his Anointed. That is what had happened in Jerusalem: Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the people of Israel, conspired against God’s holy servant Jesus, whom he anointed, doing only what God’s power and will had decided beforehand. Now they asked the Lord to consider the threats, and to enable his servants to speak his word with great boldness while he stretched out his hand to heal and perform signs and wonders through the name of his holy servant Jesus. When they had prayed, the place where they met was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke God’s word boldly. All the believers were one in heart and mind. No one claimed their possessions as their own; they shared everything. With great power the apostles continued to testify to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was on them all. There was no one needy among them, because from time to time owners of land or houses sold them and brought the money to the apostles, who distributed it to anyone in need. Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus whom the apostles called Barnabas, meaning son of encouragement, sold a field he owned and laid the money at the apostles’ feet.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sovereignty of God and Human Responsibility

Verses 27 and 28 are among the most explicit statements of divine sovereignty in the New Testament: Herod, Pontius Pilate, the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel gathered against Jesus to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place. What is striking is the setting. This is not a chapter of argument. It is a prayer, offered by frightened people the morning after a night in custody. The doctrine is not being defended here; it is being leaned on. Reformed theology has always insisted that the two truths — real human guilt and a real divine purpose — must be held together rather than traded against each other, and this chapter shows what holding them together is actually for. If the murder of the Son of God fell inside the plan, then a threat delivered that morning falls inside it too. Which is why the prayer runs straight on from verse 28 to verse 29 without a pause. The sovereignty is not the conclusion of the prayer. It is the ground they are standing on in order to ask for courage.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Luke reports the result of the church's generosity in a sentence that echoes the law of Moses: there was not a needy person among them (compare Deuteronomy 15:4). Deuteronomy had held exactly that out as a possibility, attached a condition Israel never met, and admitted in the same chapter that the poor would never cease out of the land. What fifteen centuries of covenant history had not produced, the Spirit produced in Jerusalem inside a year. Now: The particular form belonged to a moment; the open hand does not. And Luke's arrangement is worth attention — he sets the giving immediately beside the preaching, in the same paragraph, so that the community's life and the apostles' message are not two subjects but one.

verseByVerse.quote: When they were released, they went to their friends and reported what the chief priests and the elders had said to them. And when they heard it, they lifted their voices together to God and said, "Sovereign Lord, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they were released, they went to their friends and reported what the chief priests and the elders had said to them. And when they heard it, they lifted their voices together to God and said, “Sovereign Lord, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them,

When they were released, they went to their friends. “Their own”: the church.

They lifted their voices together to God. Their first response to threats: prayer, together.

Sovereign Lord. Key words. “Sovereign Lord” (Despota): master, absolute ruler. The word for a master of slaves. They begin their prayer not with their problem, but with God’s sovereignty.

Who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them. From Psalm 146:6 and Exodus 20:11. The Creator of all is greater than the council. Remembering who God is puts every threat in perspective.

In a sentence. When released, they went back to the believers and reported what had been said, and together they prayed to the Sovereign Lord who made heaven, earth, sea and everything in them.

On a Tuesday. When you are threatened, start your prayer with who God is. He made everything.

parallels.desc: who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them

verseByVerse.quote: "who through the mouth of our father David, your servant, said by the Holy Spirit, 'Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed' —"
verseByVerse.commentary:
who through the mouth of our father David, your servant, said by the Holy Spirit, ‘Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed’ —

Who through the mouth of our father David, your servant, said by the Holy Spirit. Inspiration again: God spoke, by the Spirit, through David (1:16).

Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain? Key words. Psalm 2:1–2, a royal psalm about God’s anointed king and the nations’ rebellion against him. “In vain”: their plotting is futile. God laughs at them (Psalm 2:4).

Against the Lord and against his Anointed. “His Anointed”: his Christ, his Messiah. Opposition to the Messiah is opposition to God.

In a sentence. They prayed to the God who spoke by the Spirit through David, asking why the nations rage and peoples plot in vain, and kings and rulers gather against the Lord and his Anointed.

For worship. The nations still rage, and still in vain. Christ reigns.

parallels.desc: why do the nations rage?

verseByVerse.quote: "for truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place."
verseByVerse.commentary:
for truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place.

For truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed. They apply the psalm to recent events. Jesus is God’s Anointed (Christ).

Both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel. Herod is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee (Luke 23:7–12). The kings (Herod) and rulers (Pilate), the Gentiles (Romans) and the peoples (Israel): every group in the psalm. Jew and Gentile together crucified him. All humanity is implicated.

To do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place. Key words. “Predestined” (proōrisen): decided beforehand, the word used of election in Romans 8:29–30 and Ephesians 1:5, 11. The greatest crime in history was planned by God. God’s hand (power) and plan (will) determined it. They did what they wanted, wickedly; and they did exactly what God had determined. This is God’s sovereignty over evil without being its author (2:23).

What it does not mean. It does not mean they were forced, or less guilty. They plotted freely, and were responsible. God works his perfect will through, not by excusing, human sin.

In a sentence. In this city Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, gathered against God’s holy servant Jesus, his Anointed, to do what his hand and plan had predetermined.

On a Tuesday. If God was sovereign over the cross, he is sovereign over your trouble. Nothing is outside his plan.
verseByVerse.note: Herod is Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, Lord, look upon their threats and grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness, while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, Lord, look upon their threats and grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness, while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus.

And now, Lord, look upon their threats. They don’t ask God to destroy their enemies, or to remove the danger.

And grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness. Key words. They pray for boldness to keep doing what they were forbidden to do. Not safety, but courage. “Your servants” (doulois): slaves of the Sovereign Lord.

While you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus. They ask God to keep confirming the word with signs. God did (5:12). These signs belonged to the founding era of the church, accrediting the apostles’ message.

In a sentence. They asked the Lord to consider their threats and give his servants boldness to keep speaking his word, as he stretched out his hand to heal and do signs and wonders through the name of his holy servant Jesus.

For worship. Pray this prayer: not “keep me safe,” but “make me bold.”

parallels.desc: pray that words may be given me to open my mouth boldly

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered together was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered together was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness.

The place in which they were gathered together was shaken. A sign of God’s presence and answer, as at Sinai (Exodus 19:18; Isaiah 6:4). The council could threaten; God shakes the building.

And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit. Key words. A fresh filling, not a second Pentecost. Believers who already have the Spirit can be filled again and again for new tasks (Ephesians 5:18).

And continued to speak the word of God with boldness. Prayer answered exactly. They asked for boldness and got it.

In a sentence. When they had prayed, the place where they were meeting shook, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and kept speaking God’s word boldly.

On a Tuesday. God answers prayer for boldness. Ask him, and then open your mouth.

parallels.desc: the whole mountain trembled

verseByVerse.quote: Now the full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own, but they had everything in common. And with great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own, but they had everything in common. And with great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all.

The full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul. Key words. Deep unity. Not uniformity, but shared love and purpose. Jesus’ prayer answered (John 17:21).

And no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own. They still owned things, but held them loosely, as belonging to God and available to others.

But they had everything in common. As in 2:44.

And with great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus. The central message.

And great grace was upon them all. God’s favour rested on the church. Generosity and gospel go together.

In a sentence. All the believers were one in heart and soul, and no one claimed his possessions as his own, but they shared everything, while the apostles testified powerfully to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was on them all.

For worship. Open hands and bold witness: that is what grace looks like in a church.

verseByVerse.quote: There was not a needy person among them, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what was sold and laid it at the apostles' feet, and it was distributed to each as any had need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was not a needy person among them, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what was sold and laid it at the apostles’ feet, and it was distributed to each as any had need.

There was not a needy person among them. Key words. Fulfilling Deuteronomy 15:4: there will be no poor among you. The new covenant community did what Israel was meant to do.

As many as were owners of lands or houses sold them. Again, as needs arose, voluntary (5:4).

And laid it at the apostles’ feet. Laying gifts at someone’s feet placed them under his authority to distribute. The apostles managed the fund, until the deacons took it over (6:1–6).

And it was distributed to each as any had need. Need, not equality, was the principle.

In a sentence. No one among them was in need, because those who owned land or houses sold them and laid the money at the apostles’ feet, and it was given to each as needed.

On a Tuesday. Is there need in your church that your abundance could meet?
verseByVerse.note: Laying gifts at someone’s feet placed them under his authority.

parallels.desc: there will be no poor among you

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Joseph, who was also called by the apostles Barnabas (which means son of encouragement), a Levite, a native of Cyprus, sold a field that belonged to him and brought the money and laid it at the apostles' feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus Joseph, who was also called by the apostles Barnabas (which means son of encouragement), a Levite, a native of Cyprus, sold a field that belonged to him and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet.

Thus Joseph, who was also called by the apostles Barnabas (which means son of encouragement). Key words. Barnabas will be a key figure: he vouches for Paul (9:27), encourages the church in Antioch (11:22–24), and travels with Paul (13:2). His nickname fits: he encourages. “Son of” in Hebrew means characterised by.

A Levite. Levites originally owned no land (Numbers 18:20), but by this time some did (Jeremiah 32:6–15).

A native of Cyprus. Cyprus was a large island in the eastern Mediterranean with a big Jewish community. Barnabas later evangelised there (13:4).

Sold a field that belonged to him and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet. A positive example, set beside the negative one that follows (5:1–11).

In a sentence. Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus whom the apostles called Barnabas, son of encouragement, sold a field and laid the money at the apostles’ feet.

For worship. Be a Barnabas: generous and encouraging. The church needs many.
verseByVerse.note: Cyprus was a large island in the eastern Mediterranean with a big Jewish community.

4.theology: The Sovereignty of God and Mission. The prayer of Acts 4:24–30 is a theology lecture compressed into seven verses. God is addressed as despotēs — Sovereign Lord, absolute Master — who made heaven and earth and everything in them. Herod and Pilate and the nations, in their opposition to Christ, did “whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place.” This is not fatalism; it is the Reformed doctrine of providence applied to history’s darkest moment. And the implication for mission is not paralysis but boldness: if God was sovereign over the crucifixion, he is sovereign over every threat to the gospel. The church does not need favourable conditions to advance the kingdom. It needs the Spirit and the Word. God provides both.
4.examples:
Then: A church only weeks old, under arrest, before the same council that crucified their Lord, with no legal protection, no political allies, no plan B — and they prayed for boldness and were given it. The shaking of the place was God’s receipt: prayer received, boldness granted.

Now: The church in every hostile culture faces the same fork: silence or speech, safety or boldness. The prayer of Acts 4 is still available. The God who shook that room has not grown quiet. He is still the Sovereign Lord who made heaven and earth. And he still grants boldness to those who ask for it — not because they deserve it, but because his Word must go out.

5.title: The Fear of the Lord
5.text: <sup>1</sup>But a man named Ananias, with his wife Sapphira, sold a piece of property, <sup>2</sup>and with his wife’s knowledge he kept back for himself some of the proceeds and brought only a part of it and laid it at the apostles’ feet. <sup>3</sup>But Peter said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back for yourself part of the proceeds of the land? <sup>4</sup>While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart? You have not lied to man but to God.” <sup>5</sup>When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. And great fear came upon all who heard of it. <sup>6</sup>The young men rose and wrapped him up and carried him out and buried him. <sup>7</sup>After an interval of about three hours his wife came in, not knowing what had happened. <sup>8</sup>And Peter said to her, “Tell me whether you sold the land for so much.” And she said, “Yes, for so much.” <sup>9</sup>But Peter said to her, “How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out.” <sup>10</sup>Immediately she fell down at his feet and breathed her last. When the young men came in they found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her beside her husband. <sup>11</sup>And great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard of these things. <sup>12</sup>Now many signs and wonders were regularly done among the people by the hands of the apostles. And they were all together in Solomon’s Portico. <sup>13</sup>None of the rest dared join them, but the people held them in high esteem. <sup>14</sup>And more than ever believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women, <sup>15</sup>so that they even carried out the sick into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, that as Peter came by at least his shadow might fall on some of them. <sup>16</sup>The people also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those afflicted with unclean spirits, and they were all healed. <sup>17</sup>But the high priest rose up, and all who were with him (that is, the party of the Sadducees), and filled with jealousy <sup>18</sup>they arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison. <sup>19</sup>But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and brought them out, and said, <sup>20</sup>“Go and stand in the temple and speak to the people all the words of this Life.” <sup>21</sup>And when they heard this, they entered the temple at daybreak and began to teach. Now when the high priest came, and those who were with him, they called together the council, all the senate of the people of Israel and sent to the prison to have them brought. <sup>22</sup>But when the officers came, they did not find them in the prison, so they returned and reported, <sup>23</sup>“We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we found no one inside.” <sup>24</sup>Now when the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these words, they were greatly perplexed about them, wondering what this would come to. <sup>25</sup>And someone came and told them, “Look! The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people.” <sup>26</sup>Then the captain with the officers went and brought them, but not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people. <sup>27</sup>And when they had brought them, they set them before the council. And the high priest questioned them, <sup>28</sup>saying, “We strictly charged you not to teach in this name, yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you intend to bring this man’s blood upon us.” <sup>29</sup>But Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than men. <sup>30</sup>The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree. <sup>31</sup>God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. <sup>32</sup>And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.” <sup>33</sup>When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them. <sup>34</sup>But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, stood up and gave orders to put the men outside for a little while. <sup>35</sup>And he said to them, “Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men. <sup>36</sup>For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and a number of men, about four hundred, joined him. He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing. <sup>37</sup>After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew away some of the people after him. He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. <sup>38</sup>So in the present case I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail; <sup>39</sup>but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God!” So they took his advice, <sup>40</sup>and when they had called in the apostles, they beat them and charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go. <sup>41</sup>Then they left the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. <sup>42</sup>And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus.
5.overview:
After the bright picture of Barnabas comes a dark one. Ananias and his wife Sapphira sell property and give part of the price while pretending it is the whole, wanting the reputation of generosity without the cost. Peter tells Ananias he has lied not to men but to God, and Ananias falls dead; three hours later Sapphira repeats the lie and dies too. Great fear seizes the whole church, the first time Luke uses that word for the believers. The story echoes Achan, who secretly kept back plunder when Israel entered the promised land (Joshua 7): at the start of a new work of God, sin in the camp is judged severely.

Meanwhile the apostles perform many signs, the sick are carried into the streets in the hope that even Peter’s shadow will fall on them, and multitudes of men and women believe. Jealous, the high priest has the apostles jailed, but an angel opens the doors at night and tells them to go and preach in the temple. Brought before the council again, they answer, “We must obey God rather than men,” and proclaim the risen Jesus as Leader and Saviour. The council wants to kill them, but Gamaliel, the most respected Pharisee teacher of the day, advises caution: movements of human origin fail, as those of Theudas and Judas the Galilean did, but if this is from God they cannot stop it and may find themselves fighting God. The apostles are flogged and released, and leave rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for the Name, and they keep teaching every day that Jesus is the Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Holiness and Power in the Young Church
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A man named Ananias and his wife Sapphira also sold a piece of property, but with her full knowledge he kept back part of the money and brought the rest to the apostles as if it were the whole. Peter asked him how he had let Satan fill his heart so that he lied to the Holy Spirit and kept back part of the price. The land was his to keep, and after selling it the money was at his disposal. Why had he thought of doing such a thing? He had lied not to people but to God. When Ananias heard this he fell down and died, and great fear came on everyone who heard. The young men wrapped his body, carried him out and buried him. About three hours later his wife came in, not knowing what had happened. Peter asked whether this was the price they got for the land, and she said yes. Peter asked how they could agree to test the Spirit of the Lord, and told her that the men who had buried her husband were at the door and would carry her out too. At once she fell down at his feet and died. The young men came in, found her dead, and buried her beside her husband. Great fear seized the whole church and all who heard. The apostles performed many signs and wonders among the people, and the believers all used to meet together in Solomon’s Colonnade. No one else dared join them, though the people held them in high regard. Yet more and more men and women believed in the Lord and were added to their number. People even brought the sick into the streets on beds and mats so that at least Peter’s shadow might fall on some as he passed. Crowds came from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those troubled by impure spirits, and all of them were healed.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Holiness of God and the Danger of Hypocrisy

The deaths of Ananias and Sapphira stand in a recognisable biblical pattern: when God inaugurates something holy, the first sin against it is judged with startling swiftness. Nadab and Abihu at the dawn of the priesthood (Leviticus 10), Achan at Israel's entry into the land (Joshua 7), Uzzah as the ark comes home (2 Samuel 6), and here the first hypocrisy at the birth of the church. These are representative judgements — one public sample of what all sin deserves, set down once. They are not the rule; God's ordinary way is the patient kindness meant to lead to repentance (Romans 2:4), which is precisely why the rest of us are still breathing. A God who never enforced his own holiness would not be holy, and the gospel does not lower that holiness but satisfies it, so that those in Christ may come near to the Holy One with confidence. The second half of the section shows what such a God does with a church that has learned to tremble before him: he fills it, and multiplies it, and heals through it in the open street.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A church only weeks old discovered that the Spirit who filled it also searched it — and that the same fear which drove off the hangers-on drew in multitudes.

Now: The pattern repeats wherever religious performance stands in for reality: the testimony allowed to run better than the facts, the prayer that warms when others are listening, the struggle described in the past tense because the present tense would cost too much. Two cautions belong with it. This chapter is not a lever for extracting money — Peter says the field and the proceeds were theirs. And the fear here came from what God did, not from what the leaders did; a congregation frightened of its elders has reproduced what this chapter killed, not what it created. The fear of God makes people honest. The fear of men is what made Ananias lie.

verseByVerse.quote: But a man named Ananias, with his wife Sapphira, sold a piece of property, and with his wife's knowledge he kept back for himself some of the proceeds and brought only a part of it and laid it at the apostles' feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But a man named Ananias, with his wife Sapphira, sold a piece of property, and with his wife’s knowledge he kept back for himself some of the proceeds and brought only a part of it and laid it at the apostles’ feet.

Meaning first. Acts 5 shows the church threatened from within and from without. From within, by deceit: Ananias and Sapphira lie to the Holy Spirit and die. From without, by persecution: the apostles are jailed, freed by an angel, flogged, and go away rejoicing. In both, God protects his church: by purifying it, and by preserving it. The chapter teaches the holiness of God, the reality of the Spirit’s presence, and the joy of suffering for Christ.

But a man named Ananias, with his wife Sapphira. “But”: a deliberate contrast with Barnabas (4:36–37). Ananias means “The Lord is gracious”; Sapphira, “beautiful.” Names that don’t match their deeds.

Sold a piece of property, and with his wife’s knowledge he kept back for himself some of the proceeds. Key words. “Kept back” (enosphisato): embezzled, pilfered. The same rare word is used in the Greek Old Testament of Achan, who kept back some of the devoted things at Jericho, and was put to death (Joshua 7:1). As Achan’s sin threatened Israel at the start of its life in the land, so this threatens the church at the start of its life.

And brought only a part of it and laid it at the apostles’ feet. Pretending it was the whole.

In a sentence. A man named Ananias and his wife Sapphira sold property, and with her knowledge he kept back some of the money and laid only part at the apostles’ feet.

On a Tuesday. The temptation to look more generous, more spiritual, than you really are is very old. Resist it.

parallels.desc: Achan keeps back what was devoted to God

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said, "Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back for yourself part of the proceeds of the land? While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart? You have not lied to man but to God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back for yourself part of the proceeds of the land? While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart? You have not lied to man but to God.”

Why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit? Key words. Satan filled his heart, as the Spirit filled the church (4:31). But Ananias let him; Peter asks “why.” He is responsible.

While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? Their sin was not keeping part of the money but pretending to give it all. They were free to keep the land, or to keep the money. Giving was voluntary. Private property was not abolished (2:45).

Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart? Premeditated.

You have not lied to man but to God. Key words. In v. 3 he lied “to the Holy Spirit”; here “to God.” The Holy Spirit is God. One of the clearest statements of the Spirit’s deity and personhood in Scripture. You can’t lie to a force; you lie to a person.

In a sentence. Peter asked Ananias why he let Satan fill his heart to lie to the Holy Spirit by keeping back some of the money, when the land and the money were his to keep, and said he had lied not to men but to God.

For worship. The Holy Spirit is God, present in his church. Worship him, and don’t trifle with him.
verseByVerse.note: Their sin was not keeping part of the money but pretending to give it all. Lying to the Holy Spirit is lying to God.

verseByVerse.quote: When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. And great fear came upon all who heard of it. The young men rose and wrapped him up and carried him out and buried him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. And great fear came upon all who heard of it. The young men rose and wrapped him up and carried him out and buried him.

When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. Key words. Sudden judgment. Peter doesn’t pronounce a curse; God acts. Like Nadab and Abihu, who offered unauthorised fire (Leviticus 10:1–2), or Uzzah, who touched the ark (2 Samuel 6:6–7), at the start of a new era in God’s dealings with his people. God’s holiness is shown at the beginning, as a warning for all time.

And great fear came upon all who heard of it. The purpose of the judgment.

The young men rose and wrapped him up and carried him out and buried him. Burial usually took place the same day, in that climate.

Where Christians differ: was Ananias saved? Some think this proves he was never a believer; others that a believer can be disciplined by death without losing salvation (1 Corinthians 11:30–32; 5:5). Verdict: Scripture doesn’t tell us, and we shouldn’t pretend to know. What is clear is that God takes sin in his church seriously, especially hypocrisy, and that he may discipline severely. It is not a pattern to expect in every case; it is a warning written at the church’s beginning.

In a sentence. When Ananias heard this, he fell down dead, and great fear came over everyone who heard; and the young men wrapped him up, carried him out and buried him.

On a Tuesday. God is holy. His grace is not permission to deceive. Walk before him in honesty.
verseByVerse.note: Burial usually took place the same day.

parallels.desc: Nadab and Abihu struck down

verseByVerse.quote: After an interval of about three hours his wife came in, not knowing what had happened. And Peter said to her, "Tell me whether you sold the land for so much." And she said, "Yes, for so much."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After an interval of about three hours his wife came in, not knowing what had happened. And Peter said to her, “Tell me whether you sold the land for so much.” And she said, “Yes, for so much.”

After an interval of about three hours his wife came in, not knowing what had happened. She had no idea.

Tell me whether you sold the land for so much. Peter gives her the chance to tell the truth.

And she said, “Yes, for so much.” She keeps to the lie.

In a sentence. About three hours later his wife came in, unaware, and when Peter asked whether they had sold the land for that amount, she said yes.

For worship. God often gives us a chance to come clean. Take it.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to her, "How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out." Immediately she fell down at his feet and breathed her last. When the young men came in they found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her beside her husband.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter said to her, “How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out.” Immediately she fell down at his feet and breathed her last. When the young men came in they found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her beside her husband.

How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Key words. “Test” (peirasai): to put to the test, to see how far you can go, as Israel tested God in the wilderness (Exodus 17:2; Deuteronomy 6:16). They were testing whether God would notice. A married couple agreeing together in sin: a sobering picture. A spouse’s duty is to help the other towards God, not away.

Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door. Peter knows by the Spirit what will happen.

Immediately she fell down at his feet and breathed her last. At the feet where they had laid their dishonest gift.

And buried her beside her husband. United in sin, united in death.

In a sentence. Peter asked her why they had agreed to test the Spirit of the Lord, and said those who buried her husband were at the door to carry her out, and she fell dead at his feet, and the young men buried her beside her husband.

On a Tuesday. Husbands and wives: agree together to honour God, never to deceive him.

parallels.desc: do not put the LORD your God to the test

verseByVerse.quote: And great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard of these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard of these things.

And great fear came upon the whole church. Key words. This is the first time Acts uses the word “church” (ekklēsia): the assembly, the called-out people. In the Greek Old Testament it was used of Israel assembled before God. Now it is the people of the Messiah. Fittingly, it appears with fear: the church is God’s holy temple (1 Corinthians 3:16–17).

And upon all who heard of these things. Outsiders too.

The fear of God. Not terror that drives us away, but reverence that draws us to walk carefully before him (Proverbs 9:10; 2 Corinthians 7:1; Hebrews 12:28–29). A church without the fear of God is not a happier church, but a weaker one.

In a sentence. Great fear came over the whole church and everyone who heard.

For worship. Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling (Psalm 2:11).
verseByVerse.note: This is the first time Acts uses the word “church.”

verseByVerse.quote: Now many signs and wonders were regularly done among the people by the hands of the apostles. And they were all together in Solomon's Portico.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now many signs and wonders were regularly done among the people by the hands of the apostles. And they were all together in Solomon’s Portico.

Now many signs and wonders were regularly done among the people by the hands of the apostles. Key words. God answers the prayer of 4:30. “By the hands of the apostles”: signs were the marks of apostles (2 Corinthians 12:12).

And they were all together in Solomon’s Portico. Solomon’s Portico was a covered colonnade on the east side of the temple courts, the church’s public meeting place (3:11).

In a sentence. The apostles regularly did many signs and wonders among the people, and the believers all met together in Solomon’s Portico.

For worship. God confirmed his word through the apostles. Their witness is the foundation of your faith.
verseByVerse.note: Solomon’s Portico was a covered colonnade on the east side of the temple courts.

verseByVerse.quote: None of the rest dared join them, but the people held them in high esteem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
None of the rest dared join them, but the people held them in high esteem.

None of the rest dared join them. “The rest”: outsiders, who were not believers. After Ananias and Sapphira, no one dared to join casually or falsely. The church was no place for the half-hearted.

But the people held them in high esteem. They respected them from a distance.

In a sentence. None of the others dared to join them, though the people thought highly of them.

On a Tuesday. A holy church may be respected and feared before it is joined. That is better than a church that is joined because it is taken lightly.

verseByVerse.quote: And more than ever believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And more than ever believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women,

And more than ever believers were added to the Lord. Key words. The paradox: no one joined lightly, yet more than ever believed. Holiness didn’t shrink the church; it grew it. “Added to the Lord”: not just to a group, but to Christ himself.

Multitudes of both men and women. Luke often notes women among the believers (8:12; 16:13–15; 17:4, 12). The gospel was for both alike.

In a sentence. More and more believers were added to the Lord, crowds of both men and women.

For worship. Purity and growth go together. Pray for both in your church.

verseByVerse.quote: so that they even carried out the sick into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, that as Peter came by at least his shadow might fall on some of them. The people also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those afflicted with unclean spirits, and they were all healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
so that they even carried out the sick into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, that as Peter came by at least his shadow might fall on some of them. The people also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those afflicted with unclean spirits, and they were all healed.

That as Peter came by at least his shadow might fall on some of them. Key words. Ancient people often believed a person’s shadow carried their power. Luke doesn’t say the shadow healed anyone; he reports what people hoped. God was gracious to their imperfect faith, as with the woman who touched Jesus’ garment (Luke 8:44) and the handkerchiefs from Paul (19:11–12). The power was God’s, not Peter’s shadow.

The people also gathered from the towns around Jerusalem. The word spreads beyond Jerusalem, as Jesus said (1:8).

And they were all healed. All, as in Jesus’ ministry (Luke 4:40; 6:19). An extraordinary season.

Where Christians differ: relics and holy objects. Some have used verses like this to support venerating relics or objects linked with saints. Verdict: Luke reports, he doesn’t prescribe. The healing came from the risen Christ, who was confirming his apostles’ message. The New Testament never teaches believers to seek power through objects, shadows or relics, and the apostles would have been horrified to be venerated (14:14–15). Look to Christ, not to his servants or their belongings.

In a sentence. People carried the sick into the streets on beds and mats hoping that even Peter’s shadow might fall on them, and crowds came from towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and the demonised, and all were healed.

On a Tuesday. God is gracious even to imperfect faith. But fix your faith on Christ himself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The high priest and his Sadducee allies, filled with jealousy, arrested the apostles and put them in the public jail. But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors, brought them out and told them to go, stand in the temple courts and tell the people all about this new life. At daybreak they did so. When the high priest convened the full council and sent for the prisoners, the officers found the jail securely locked with guards at the doors but no one inside. While the leaders were puzzling over this, someone reported that the men were standing in the temple teaching the people. The captain went with his officers and brought them, without force, fearing the crowd would stone them. The high priest reminded them of the strict order not to teach in this name, and accused them of filling Jerusalem with their teaching and trying to make the leaders guilty of this man’s blood. Peter and the apostles replied that they must obey God rather than human beings. The God of their ancestors raised Jesus, whom the leaders killed by hanging him on a cross; God exalted him to his right hand as Prince and Saviour, to bring Israel to repentance and forgive their sins. The apostles are witnesses, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God gives to those who obey him. Furious, the council wanted to put them to death. But Gamaliel, a Pharisee and respected teacher of the law, had the men put outside and warned the council to be careful. Theudas had claimed to be somebody and gathered about four hundred men, but he was killed and his followers scattered; Judas the Galilean led a revolt at the time of the census and he too perished. So they should leave these men alone: if their plan is of human origin it will fail, but if it is from God they will not be able to stop them and may find themselves fighting against God. The council agreed, had the apostles flogged, ordered them not to speak in Jesus’ name, and let them go. The apostles left rejoicing that they had been counted worthy of suffering disgrace for the Name, and day after day, in the temple courts and from house to house, they never stopped teaching and proclaiming the good news that Jesus is the Messiah.
verseByVerse.theology:
Obeying God Rather Than Men

Gamaliel's advice — if it is of man it will fail, if it is of God you cannot overthrow it — is often praised as tolerance. It is not Christian reasoning. It is pragmatic patience that never distinguishes truth from falsehood, only durable movements from short-lived ones, and it allows a man to avoid the one question in the room: did God raise Jesus? He is a providential restraint, not a theological authority. The apostles rest their case on something else entirely. Their principle is not defiance but a hierarchy of obedience: the state's authority is real and derived, and a delegated authority that forbids what God commands has run out of warrant at that point and no further. The same New Testament that records these words commands submission to governing authorities under Nero (Romans 13:1; 1 Peter 2:13-17). And the apostles supply the test that keeps the principle honest — they did not resist arrest, did not raise the crowd that was ready to riot for them, and did not flee. They took the flogging. Biblical civil disobedience characteristically accepts the penalty rather than looking for an escape clause.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The apostles left the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the Name — led by the man who, only months earlier, had denied that he knew Jesus to a servant girl beside a fire. What changed was not his temperament.

Now: Suffering for the Name is not masochism and joy in it is not a duty to be manufactured in advance; it was given to those men on the way out of the building. Two things this passage is not: it is not a text to hand a grieving or ill person, since the suffering in view is dishonour incurred for Christ; and it is not a slogan for defying laws one merely dislikes. The question is always whether God is being forbidden what he commands — and whether one is prepared to bear the cost of saying so.

verseByVerse.quote: But the high priest rose up, and all who were with him (that is, the party of the Sadducees), and filled with jealousy they arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the high priest rose up, and all who were with him (that is, the party of the Sadducees), and filled with jealousy they arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison.

But the high priest rose up, and all who were with him (that is, the party of the Sadducees). The second attack.

And filled with jealousy. Key words. “Jealousy” (zēlou): envy, zeal. The real motive: the apostles were more popular than they were. The same motive that handed Jesus over (Mark 15:10).

They arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison. All the apostles this time, not just Peter and John.

In a sentence. The high priest and his Sadducee party, filled with jealousy, arrested the apostles and put them in the public jail.

For worship. Envy hates the blessing of others. Pray to rejoice when God blesses someone else.

verseByVerse.quote: But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and brought them out, and said, "Go and stand in the temple and speak to the people all the words of this Life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and brought them out, and said, “Go and stand in the temple and speak to the people all the words of this Life.”

But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and brought them out. Key words. The Sadducees, who denied angels (23:8), are thwarted by one. God mocks their unbelief. Angels are ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14).

Go and stand in the temple and speak to the people. Not “escape and hide,” but “go back to the place of danger and preach.” Release is for mission.

All the words of this Life. “This Life”: the gospel is a message of life, the new life in Christ that the Sadducees denied.

In a sentence. During the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors, brought them out, and told them to go stand in the temple and tell the people all about this new life.

On a Tuesday. When God rescues you, it’s often to send you back to speak.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they heard this, they entered the temple at daybreak and began to teach. Now when the high priest came, and those who were with him, they called together the council, all the senate of the people of Israel, and sent to the prison to have them brought.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they heard this, they entered the temple at daybreak and began to teach. Now when the high priest came, and those who were with him, they called together the council, all the senate of the people of Israel, and sent to the prison to have them brought.

They entered the temple at daybreak and began to teach. Immediate obedience, at the first hour of public activity.

They called together the council, all the senate of the people of Israel. The council is the Sanhedrin. “Senate” (gerousia): council of elders. A full, formal session.

And sent to the prison to have them brought. The comic irony begins.

In a sentence. They went into the temple at dawn and began teaching, while the high priest called a full session of the council and sent to the prison to have them brought.

For worship. The council assembled to judge the apostles, who were already free and preaching. God laughs at those who oppose him (Psalm 2:4).
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the officers came, they did not find them in the prison, so they returned and reported, "We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we found no one inside."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when the officers came, they did not find them in the prison, so they returned and reported, “We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we found no one inside.”

We found the prison securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them we found no one inside. Locked doors, guards in place, cells empty. Like the empty tomb, with guards and seal. No human explanation.

In a sentence. The officers didn’t find them in the prison, and reported that it was securely locked with the guards at the doors, but no one was inside.

On a Tuesday. No locked door can keep in those God wants out.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these words, they were greatly perplexed about them, wondering what this would come to. And someone came and told them, "Look! The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when the captain of the temple and the chief priests heard these words, they were greatly perplexed about them, wondering what this would come to. And someone came and told them, “Look! The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people.”

They were greatly perplexed about them, wondering what this would come to. “Perplexed” (diēporoun): at a total loss. They have lost control.

The men whom you put in prison are standing in the temple and teaching the people. Back at work, a few hundred yards away.

In a sentence. The captain and chief priests were completely baffled, wondering where this would lead, until someone told them the men they had jailed were in the temple teaching the people.

For worship. The gospel keeps breaking out. Opposition only spreads it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the captain with the officers went and brought them, but not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people. And when they had brought them, they set them before the council.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the captain with the officers went and brought them, but not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people. And when they had brought them, they set them before the council.

But not by force, for they were afraid of being stoned by the people. The apostles come willingly. The authorities fear the people.

They set them before the council. The apostles could have resisted with the crowd’s help. They didn’t. They submit to arrest, and then refuse to submit on the question of preaching.

In a sentence. The captain and his officers brought them without force, fearing the people would stone them, and set them before the council.

On a Tuesday. Christians don’t use mob power to resist authorities. They submit where they can, and obey God where they must.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest questioned them, saying, "We strictly charged you not to teach in this name, yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you intend to bring this man's blood upon us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the high priest questioned them, saying, “We strictly charged you not to teach in this name, yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you intend to bring this man’s blood upon us.”

We strictly charged you not to teach in this name. Again he avoids saying the name of Jesus.

Yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching. An unintended compliment.

And you intend to bring this man’s blood upon us. Key words. The irony: at Jesus’ trial, the crowd cried, “His blood be on us and on our children” (Matthew 27:25). Now the leaders are afraid of being held responsible. But the apostles offer the very blood they fear as the means of forgiveness (Hebrews 12:24).

In a sentence. The high priest said they had been strictly ordered not to teach in this name, yet had filled Jerusalem with their teaching and intended to make the leaders guilty of this man’s blood.

For worship. The blood they feared is the blood that cleanses. Plead it for yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter and the apostles answered, "We must obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree.

We must obey God rather than men. Key words. The principle of 4:19, now stated as a short, clear rule. “Must” (dei): it is necessary. When a human command conflicts with God’s, God wins. The motto of martyrs through the centuries.

The God of our fathers raised Jesus. Not a foreign God, but Israel’s God.

Whom you killed by hanging him on a tree. Being hung on a tree was under God’s curse in the law (Deuteronomy 21:22–23). The leaders meant to show Jesus was cursed by God. The apostles show that he bore the curse for us (Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24).

In a sentence. Peter and the apostles answered that they must obey God rather than men, and that the God of their fathers raised Jesus, whom the leaders had killed by hanging him on a tree.

For worship. Christ hung on the tree under the curse, so that the curse would never fall on you.
verseByVerse.note: Being hung on a tree was under God’s curse in the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.

God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior. Key words. “Leader” (archēgon): prince, pioneer, author (3:15). “Savior” (sōtēra): rescuer. Titles that the Old Testament gives to God (Isaiah 43:11).

To give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. Key words. Christ gives repentance. Not only forgiveness, but repentance itself is his gift (11:18; 2 Timothy 2:25). We cannot produce it on our own. And yet we are commanded to repent (3:19). Both are true.

And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit. Two witnesses: the apostles and the Spirit (John 15:26–27). The Spirit bears witness through the signs and through the change in believers.

Whom God has given to those who obey him. “Obey” here means obey the gospel, believe (6:7; Romans 1:5; 2 Thessalonians 1:8). Not that the Spirit is earned by obedience, but that he is given to those who submit to God’s call to repent and believe.

In a sentence. God exalted Jesus to his right hand as Leader and Saviour to give Israel repentance and forgiveness, and the apostles and the Holy Spirit, given to those who obey God, are witnesses.

On a Tuesday. Ask Christ for repentance. It is his gift to give.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them. But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, stood up and gave orders to put the men outside for a little while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they heard this, they were enraged and wanted to kill them. But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, stood up and gave orders to put the men outside for a little while.

They were enraged and wanted to kill them. “Enraged” (dieprionto): literally sawn through, cut to the quick. Contrast those “cut to the heart” at Pentecost (2:37), who repented. The same word can produce repentance or rage.

But a Pharisee in the council named Gamaliel. Setting and background. Gamaliel was the most respected Pharisee teacher of the day, grandson of the great rabbi Hillel, and Paul’s teacher (22:3). The Mishnah says that when he died, the glory of the law ceased. The Pharisees were a minority in the council, but popular with the people.

And gave orders to put the men outside for a little while. A private discussion.

In a sentence. When they heard this, they were furious and wanted to kill them, but Gamaliel, a Pharisee teacher of the law honoured by all the people, stood up and ordered the men to be put outside for a while.

For worship. God can raise up an unexpected voice to protect his people. He rules over councils.
verseByVerse.note: Gamaliel was the most respected Pharisee teacher of the day, and Paul’s teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men. For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and a number of men, about four hundred, joined him. He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to them, “Men of Israel, take care what you are about to do with these men. For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and a number of men, about four hundred, joined him. He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing.

Take care what you are about to do with these men. A call to caution.

For before these days Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody. Theudas is otherwise unknown from this period; Josephus mentions a Theudas who led a revolt about AD 45, about ten years after this speech. Either Gamaliel refers to an earlier Theudas, a common name, or Josephus is mistaken in his dating. There were many such rebels in those years; Josephus says the land was full of them. There is no reason to doubt Luke’s accuracy, which has been confirmed many times elsewhere.

He was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and came to nothing. His movement died with him.

In a sentence. Gamaliel told them to be careful what they did, for Theudas had once claimed to be somebody and gathered about four hundred followers, but he was killed and his movement came to nothing.

On a Tuesday. Many movements claiming to be from God die with their leaders. Christ’s did not, because he rose.
verseByVerse.note: Theudas is otherwise unknown from this period; Josephus mentions a later rebel of the same name.

verseByVerse.quote: "After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew away some of the people after him. He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. So in the present case I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census and drew away some of the people after him. He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. So in the present case I tell you, keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail;

After him Judas the Galilean rose up in the days of the census. Judas the Galilean led a revolt against the Roman census of AD 6 (Josephus confirms it), teaching that paying taxes to Rome was slavery and that God alone was king. His movement fed the later Zealots.

He too perished, and all who followed him were scattered. Another failed messiah.

Keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail. Key words. Gamaliel’s principle: time will tell. Human movements fail.

In a sentence. Gamaliel said Judas the Galilean also rose up at the time of the census and led people away, but he died and his followers scattered, so they should leave these men alone, for if this plan was of human origin it would fail.

For worship. Human plans fail. God’s purpose stands for ever (Isaiah 46:10).
verseByVerse.note: Judas the Galilean led a revolt against the Roman census of AD 6.

verseByVerse.quote: "but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God!" So they took his advice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God!” So they took his advice.

But if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. True, and Luke’s whole book proves it.

You might even be found opposing God! “Opposing God” (theomachoi): fighters against God. Gamaliel’s own pupil, Saul, would soon do exactly that, and discover it (26:14).

Where Christians differ: is Gamaliel’s test reliable? Some treat it as a sure rule: if something succeeds, it is from God. Verdict: it is wise caution, and true in the long run, but not a full test. False religions have lasted centuries, and God’s work can look as if it is failing for a time. The true test is Scripture and Christ (1 John 4:1–3). Gamaliel’s advice was sensible, but it was neutrality, not faith. Neutrality towards Christ is not enough.

So they took his advice. For now.

In a sentence. Gamaliel said that if it was of God they could not overthrow them, and might even find themselves fighting against God, and the council accepted his advice.

On a Tuesday. Waiting to see whether Christ is real is not enough. He is. Decide.

verseByVerse.quote: and when they had called in the apostles, they beat them and charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and when they had called in the apostles, they beat them and charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.

They beat them. The beating was probably the synagogue punishment of thirty-nine lashes (Deuteronomy 25:3; 2 Corinthians 11:24), a brutal flogging. Jesus had warned them: they will flog you in their synagogues (Matthew 10:17).

And charged them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go. The same command as before. It will have the same effect.

In a sentence. They called the apostles in, had them flogged, ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and released them.

For worship. The first apostles bled for the name. Honour them by speaking it.
verseByVerse.note: The beating was probably the synagogue punishment of thirty-nine lashes.

parallels.desc: forty stripes

verseByVerse.quote: Then they left the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they left the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. And every day, in the temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus.

Rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. Key words. Joy after a flogging. Not because pain is good, but because suffering for Christ is an honour (Matthew 5:11–12; 1 Peter 4:13–16; Philippians 1:29). “The name”: no need to say whose. Within a few years Christians spoke of “the name” as a title for Jesus (3 John 7).

And every day, in the temple and from house to house. Public and private: in the temple courts and in homes. The pattern of ministry (20:20).

They did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus. “Preaching” (euangelizomenoi): proclaiming the good news. The heart of it: the Messiah is Jesus.

In a sentence. They left the council rejoicing that they had been considered worthy to suffer disgrace for the name, and every day in the temple and in homes they kept teaching and proclaiming that Jesus is the Christ.

On a Tuesday. If you are mocked for Christ today, count it an honour. Then keep speaking of him.

5.theology: The Holiness of God in the New Covenant Community. The deaths of Ananias and Sapphira are not anomalies — they have a precise parallel in Leviticus 10, where Nadab and Abihu are struck dead at the founding of the tabernacle worship. At every founding moment of a new covenant expression, God makes his holiness unmistakable. He did it at Sinai. He did it in the wilderness. He does it here, at the birth of the church. The message is the same: I am holy. You are dwelling in the presence of the Holy One. This is not a place for pretence. It is not that God is more severe in the new covenant than the old; it is that the new covenant community lives in an even closer proximity to the Holy Spirit than any previous generation, and proximity to holiness demands purity.
5.examples:
Then: A Jerusalem church only weeks old, discovering that the Spirit who fills them also searches them — and that the God of grace is also the God of holiness. The fear that fell on the church was not paralyzing; a few verses later we are told that believers were added to the Lord in multitudes. Healthy fear of God does not drive people away from him; it drives away the casual, and draws in the sincere.

Now: The contemporary church has largely lost the category of the fear of God. We speak of grace, love, and welcome — and rightly so. But a church that never trembles before the holiness of God has not understood grace; it has domesticated it. Ananias and Sapphira remind every generation that the Spirit cannot be fooled, that the church is not a social club, and that God’s presence is still a consuming fire.

6.title: The Choosing of the Seven
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Now in these days when the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint by the Hellenists arose against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution. <sup>2</sup>And the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples and said, “It is not right that we should give up preaching the word of God to serve tables. <sup>3</sup>Therefore, brothers, pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we will appoint to this duty. <sup>4</sup>But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.” <sup>5</sup>And what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. <sup>6</sup>These they set before the apostles, and they prayed and laid their hands on them. <sup>7</sup>And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith. <sup>8</sup>And Stephen, full of grace and power, was doing great wonders and signs among the people. <sup>9</sup>Then some of those who belonged to the synagogue of the Freedmen (as it was called), and of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and
