Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias.” And he said, “Here I am, Lord.” And the Lord said to him, “Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul, for behold, he is praying,

Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. An ordinary believer, devout according to the law and well spoken of by the Jews (22:12). Not the Ananias of chapter 5.

Here I am, Lord. Like Samuel (1 Samuel 3:10) and Isaiah (Isaiah 6:8). Ready.

Go to the street called Straight. Straight Street still runs east–west through the old city of Damascus, the main street with colonnades. A precise, verifiable detail.

At the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul. Tarsus, his home city, in Cilicia (21:39).

For behold, he is praying. Key words. The proof of change. Saul had prayed all his life as a Pharisee. Now he prays as a broken man to the risen Jesus.

In a sentence. There was a disciple in Damascus named Ananias, and the Lord called him in a vision, and he answered, and the Lord told him to go to Straight Street, to Judas’s house, and ask for Saul of Tarsus, who was praying.

On a Tuesday. God uses ordinary believers for extraordinary tasks. Be ready to say, “Here I am, Lord.”
verseByVerse.note: Straight Street still runs east–west through the old city of Damascus. Tarsus was a major city in Cilicia, known for learning.

verseByVerse.quote: and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight.”

He has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him. Two visions, matching. God prepares both sides of the meeting, as he will with Peter and Cornelius (chapter 10).

So that he might regain his sight. Physical healing, and a sign of spiritual sight.

In a sentence. Saul had seen in a vision a man named Ananias come and lay hands on him to restore his sight.

For worship. God works on both ends: preparing hearts to hear, and messengers to speak.

verseByVerse.quote: But Ananias answered, "Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.”

Lord, I have heard from many about this man. Understandable fear. Saul’s reputation had reached Damascus.

How much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. Key words. “Saints” means those set apart as God’s holy people: all believers, not a special class (Romans 1:7; 1 Corinthians 1:2). The first time Acts uses the word. “Your saints”: they belong to Jesus.

And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name. “Call on your name”: Christians are those who call on Jesus as Lord (2:21; Romans 10:13; 1 Corinthians 1:2). Prayer to Jesus marked them out.

Where Christians differ: who are the saints? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches use “saints” mainly for specially holy people, canonised after death, whose prayers are sought. Verdict: in the New Testament every believer is a saint, set apart by God in Christ (Ephesians 1:1; Philippians 1:1). Holiness of life should follow, but the title is given by grace, not earned. We pray to God alone, through Christ alone.

In a sentence. Ananias objected that he had heard how much harm Saul had done to the Lord’s saints in Jerusalem, and that he had authority from the chief priests to arrest all who call on the Lord’s name.

On a Tuesday. If you belong to Christ, you are a saint. Live like one.
verseByVerse.note: “Saints” means those set apart as God’s holy people — all believers.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord said to him, "Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the Lord said to him, “Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name.”

Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine. Key words. “Chosen” (eklogēs): election. Saul was chosen by Christ before he knew it (Galatians 1:15). “Instrument” (skeuos): vessel, tool. God uses him as his tool. Not because he was good, but because God chose him (1 Corinthians 15:9–10).

To carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. The outline of Paul’s ministry: Gentiles (13:46–48), kings (Agrippa, 26:1; and Caesar), and Israel (in every synagogue). He will carry the name as one carries a precious vessel.

For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name. Key words. The persecutor will be persecuted. He who made believers suffer will suffer for Christ (2 Corinthians 11:23–28). Not as punishment, but as the cost of carrying the name. “Must” (dei): divinely necessary.

In a sentence. The Lord told Ananias to go, for Saul was his chosen instrument to carry his name before Gentiles, kings and Israel, and he would show Saul how much he must suffer for his name.

For worship. Christ chooses his instruments by grace, and calls them to suffer for his name. It is an honour.

verseByVerse.quote: So Ananias departed and entered the house. And laying his hands on him he said, "Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit." And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. Then he rose and was baptized;
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Ananias departed and entered the house. And laying his hands on him he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. Then he rose and was baptized;

So Ananias departed and entered the house. Obedience despite fear.

Brother Saul. Key words. Two of the most beautiful words in Acts. The man who came to arrest believers is welcomed as a brother. Grace makes enemies family.

The Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me. Ananias confirms that it was Jesus who appeared.

So that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit. Sight restored, and the Spirit given. Here not through an apostle, but through an ordinary disciple. There is no fixed pattern requiring apostles for the Spirit to be given.

Something like scales fell from his eyes. Luke the doctor’s description. We still say “the scales fell from my eyes.”

Then he rose and was baptized. At once. Baptism follows faith.

In a sentence. Ananias went into the house, laid hands on him and called him Brother Saul, saying the Lord Jesus who appeared to him on the road had sent him so that Saul would see again and be filled with the Spirit, and at once something like scales fell from his eyes, he could see, and he got up and was baptised.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone you find hard to call “brother” or “sister”? Grace calls you to.

verseByVerse.quote: and taking food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, "He is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and taking food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, “He is the Son of God.”

And taking food, he was strengthened. After three days’ fast.

For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. The people he came to arrest became his family.

And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues. The very synagogues to which he had letters to arrest believers. Paul says he also went to Arabia (the Nabataean kingdom) before returning to Damascus (Galatians 1:17). Luke compresses the time.

He is the Son of God. Key words. The only time in Acts that “Son of God” is used in preaching (but compare 13:33). The first thing Paul preached: Jesus is the Son of God. Exactly the claim for which the council condemned Jesus (Luke 22:70–71).

In a sentence. He ate and regained his strength, stayed some days with the disciples in Damascus, and at once began proclaiming in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God.

For worship. The first message of the converted persecutor: Jesus is the Son of God. Let it be yours.
verseByVerse.note: Paul says he also went to Arabia (the Nabataean kingdom) before returning to Damascus.

verseByVerse.quote: And all who heard him were amazed and said, "Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?" But Saul increased all the more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all who heard him were amazed and said, “Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?” But Saul increased all the more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ.

Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? “Made havoc” (porthēsas): destroyed, ravaged. Paul uses the same word of himself (Galatians 1:13, 23).

But Saul increased all the more in strength. Growing in power and confidence.

And confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ. Key words. “Proving” (symbibazōn): bringing together, putting the pieces side by side. He laid Scripture and the facts of Jesus’ life together and showed that they fit. A brilliant scholar of the law, he now used all his learning for Christ.

In a sentence. Everyone who heard him was amazed, asking if this wasn’t the man who had wrecked the Jerusalem believers and come here to arrest them, but Saul grew stronger and baffled the Jews in Damascus by proving that Jesus is the Christ.

On a Tuesday. God can use your training, your mind and your past for his glory. Offer them to him.

verseByVerse.quote: When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him,

When many days had passed. “Many days” probably covers about three years (Galatians 1:18). Paul adds that the governor under King Aretas guarded the city to seize him (2 Corinthians 11:32). The Jews and the Nabataean authorities worked together.

The Jews plotted to kill him. The hunter becomes the hunted. The suffering Jesus promised begins (v. 16).

They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him. The city was sealed.

In a sentence. After a long time the Jews plotted to kill him, but Saul learned of it, as they watched the gates day and night to kill him.

For worship. The persecutor became the persecuted. Suffering for Christ is the badge of his servants.
verseByVerse.note: “Many days” probably covers about three years. Paul adds that the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city.

verseByVerse.quote: but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket.
verseByVerse.commentary:
but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket.

His disciples took him by night. “His disciples”: people he had won to Christ. Already he had followers.

And let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket. Key words. A humiliating escape, like Rahab’s spies (Joshua 2:15). Paul later boasts of it as an example of his weakness (2 Corinthians 11:30–33). The great Pharisee, who came with letters of authority, leaves in a basket in the dark. God humbles his servants.

In a sentence. But his disciples took him at night and lowered him in a basket through an opening in the wall.

On a Tuesday. God’s servants are not too proud for the basket. Boast in your weakness, and in Christ’s strength.

parallels.desc: let down in a basket through a window in the wall

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.

He attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him. Understandable. Was it a trick?

But Barnabas took him. Key words. Barnabas was a respected believer from Cyprus (4:36). The son of encouragement lives up to his name. He takes a risk on the former persecutor. Without Barnabas, Paul might never have been accepted. Later Barnabas would take a risk on John Mark too (15:37–39).

And brought him to the apostles. Peter and James (Galatians 1:18–19). Paul stayed with Peter fifteen days.

And declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord. Barnabas vouches for him.

In a sentence. When Saul came to Jerusalem and tried to join the disciples, they were all afraid of him, not believing he was a disciple, but Barnabas brought him to the apostles and told them how he had seen the Lord on the road and preached boldly in Damascus.

On a Tuesday. Be a Barnabas. Take a risk on someone others are wary of. Vouch for the new believer.
verseByVerse.note: Barnabas was a respected believer from Cyprus.

parallels.desc: Paul visits Cephas and James

verseByVerse.quote: So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. But they were seeking to kill him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. But they were seeking to kill him.

So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem. Accepted, moving freely among the believers.

Preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. Boldness, the mark of the Spirit-filled witness.

And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. The Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jews: the group that had opposed Stephen (6:9). Saul, perhaps once one of them, now takes up Stephen’s argument, in the same synagogues. Stephen’s mantle falls on the man who held the coats.

But they were seeking to kill him. As they had killed Stephen.

In a sentence. So Saul moved freely among them in Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the Lord’s name, and debated with the Greek-speaking Jews, who tried to kill him.

For worship. God raised up a Stephen from the man who watched Stephen die. He always finishes his work.
verseByVerse.note: The Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jews — the group that had opposed Stephen.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.

When the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus. Caesarea was the port; Tarsus was Paul’s home city, in Cilicia. Jesus also told him in a vision to leave Jerusalem, for they would not accept his testimony (22:17–21). He spent about ten years in Syria and Cilicia (Galatians 1:21), largely hidden from history, before Barnabas fetched him to Antioch (11:25–26). Years of preparation.

In a sentence. When the believers heard, they took him down to Caesarea and sent him to Tarsus.

On a Tuesday. God’s great servants often have hidden years. If you are in one, he is preparing you.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea was the port; Tarsus was Paul’s home city.

parallels.desc: the regions of Syria and Cilicia

verseByVerse.quote: So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up. And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up. And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied.

So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace. Key words. “Church” singular: one church across three regions. With the chief persecutor converted, peace came.

And was being built up. Strengthened, edified.

And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied. Key words. Fear and comfort together: reverence for the Lord and encouragement from the Spirit. A healthy church has both. And it grew. Another of Luke’s progress reports (6:7).

In a sentence. So the church throughout Judea, Galilee and Samaria had peace and was strengthened, and living in the fear of the Lord and the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it grew in numbers.

For worship. Pray for your church to walk in the fear of the Lord and the comfort of the Spirit. Growth follows.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–43 — Peter's Ministry in Lydda and Joppa
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As Peter travelled about the country, he went to visit the Lord’s people in Lydda. There he found a man named Aeneas, paralysed and bedridden for eight years. Peter told him that Jesus Christ was healing him and to get up and roll up his mat, and Aeneas got up at once. Everyone in Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord. In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha (in Greek, Dorcas), always doing good and helping the poor. She became ill and died, and her body was washed and laid in an upstairs room. Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples sent two men to urge Peter to come at once. When he arrived he was taken upstairs, where all the widows stood around him crying and showing him the robes and other clothing Dorcas had made while she was with them. Peter sent them all out, knelt and prayed. Turning to the body, he said, “Tabitha, get up.” She opened her eyes, saw Peter and sat up. He took her hand and helped her to her feet, then called the believers, especially the widows, and presented her to them alive. This became known all over Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. Peter stayed in Joppa for some time with a tanner named Simon.
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection as the Power Behind Healing and New Life

The raising of Tabitha is told in a way that deliberately recalls the raising of Jairus's daughter — the mourners put outside, the taking of the hand, the command to rise, the girl presented back to her people. Peter is not improvising, and he is not exercising a power of his own; he is doing what he had watched being done, in the name of the one who did it and who was himself raised afterwards. That is why he kneels first. Reformed theology has read every healing and raising in Acts as a sign rather than a policy: a working sample of the new creation, offered in advance and on a small scale, of the day when everything sin and death have broken is put right permanently. Which is also why these events are rare rather than routine even in Acts. A sign that happened every time would not be a sign; it would be the arrangement, and the arrangement is still to come.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: When Tabitha died, the widows stood in the room holding up the coats and the dresses she had made, and Luke notes that she had made them while she was with them. That is what her ministry consisted of, and it is what the church had to show for her. Now: It is worth asking what would be held up. Not what would be said at the service, which is a different question and easier — but what could be carried into the room and shown.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as Peter went here and there among them all, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now as Peter went here and there among them all, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed.

Now as Peter went here and there among them all. Visiting the churches.

He came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. Lydda (modern Lod) lay about 25 miles north-west of Jerusalem, on the road to Joppa. Believers were already there, probably from Philip’s preaching (8:40).

A man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed. A Greek name, perhaps a Hellenist believer.

In a sentence. As Peter travelled about, he went to the saints in Lydda, where he found a man named Aeneas, paralysed and bedridden for eight years.

On a Tuesday. Visit the sick and the shut-in. Peter went to them.
verseByVerse.note: Lydda (modern Lod) lay about 25 miles north-west of Jerusalem, on the road to the coast.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said to him, "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed." And immediately he rose. And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Peter said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed.” And immediately he rose. And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.

Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Key words. Not “I heal you,” but “Jesus Christ heals you.” Present tense: he is healing you now. Peter is only the messenger.

Rise and make your bed. Or “prepare a meal for yourself,” possible in Greek. Do for yourself what others have done for you.

And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord. Sharon was the fertile coastal plain. “All” is a generalisation: many. The sign led to faith.

In a sentence. Peter told him that Jesus Christ was healing him and to get up and make his bed, and at once he got up, and everyone in Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord.

For worship. Jesus Christ heals. Give him the glory for every healing.
verseByVerse.note: Sharon was the fertile coastal plain.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. In those days she became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. In those days she became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.

Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha. Joppa (modern Jaffa) was the port from which Jonah sailed to flee from God’s call to the Gentiles (Jonah 1:3). Here Peter will receive his call to the Gentiles (chapter 10). “Disciple” (mathētria): the feminine form, used only here in the New Testament.

Which, translated, means Dorcas. Tabitha in Aramaic, Dorcas in Greek: both mean gazelle.

She was full of good works and acts of charity. Key words. “Full of”: she overflowed with practical kindness. Faith working through love (Galatians 5:6; James 2:17).

She became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room. Normal preparation for burial. Not anointed or buried yet: they hoped.

In a sentence. In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha, or Dorcas, who was always doing good and helping the poor, but she became ill and died, and they washed her body and laid it in an upstairs room.

On a Tuesday. Be full of good works. A life of quiet kindness is precious to God.
verseByVerse.note: Joppa (modern Jaffa) was the port from which Jonah sailed. Tabitha (Aramaic) and Dorcas (Greek) both mean “gazelle.”

verseByVerse.quote: Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him, "Please come to us without delay."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him, “Please come to us without delay.”

Since Lydda was near Joppa. Lydda was about 11 miles from Joppa, a few hours’ walk.

Please come to us without delay. Faith expecting something. They had heard of Aeneas.

In a sentence. Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing Peter was there, sent two men to urge him to come at once.

For worship. In your grief, send for help. God uses his people to comfort and strengthen.
verseByVerse.note: Lydda was about 11 miles from Joppa.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. But Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, "Tabitha, arise." And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. But Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, “Tabitha, arise.” And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up.

All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made. Key words. A touching scene. The widows she clothed show her handiwork. Her love was made visible in clothes. Many church sewing groups since have been named after her.

But Peter put them all outside. As Jesus did with Jairus’s daughter (Mark 5:40). Peter had been there.

And knelt down and prayed. Peter has no power of his own. He prays.

Tabitha, arise. In Aramaic, “Tabitha, koum,” only one letter different from Jesus’ words to Jairus’s daughter, Talitha, koum (Mark 5:41). Peter does what he saw Jesus do, by Jesus’ power.

And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up. Simple, vivid detail.

In a sentence. Peter went with them to the upstairs room, where the widows stood weeping and showing him clothes Dorcas had made, but he sent them out, knelt and prayed, and turning to the body said, “Tabitha, get up,” and she opened her eyes, saw Peter and sat up.

For worship. The Lord of life works through his servants’ prayers. Kneel before you speak.

parallels.desc: “Talitha cumi”

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave her his hand and raised her up. Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he gave her his hand and raised her up. Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive.

And he gave her his hand and raised her up. As Peter did for the lame man (3:7), and Jesus for Peter’s mother-in-law (Mark 1:31).

Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive. Key words. “Presented her alive”: the same phrase as Jesus presenting himself alive (1:3). A picture of resurrection, and of the joy of the last day, when Christ will present his people alive.

In a sentence. He gave her his hand, helped her up, and calling the saints and widows, presented her to them alive.

On a Tuesday. One day Christ will take your hand and raise you, and present you alive to all his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.

And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. Again, a sign leads to faith.

And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner. Key words. Tanners handled the skins of dead animals, a trade many Jews considered unclean, because of contact with carcasses (Leviticus 11:39–40). Tanners had to live outside towns because of the smell. Peter staying with a tanner shows his scruples were already loosening. God was preparing him for the next step: the Gentile Cornelius, whose messengers will find him in this house (10:6).

In a sentence. This became known all over Joppa, and many believed in the Lord, and Peter stayed there many days with a tanner named Simon.

For worship. God moves his servants step by step past their prejudices. Let him move you.
verseByVerse.note: Tanners handled the skins of dead animals, a trade many Jews regarded as unclean — a hint of the lesson Peter is about to learn.

9.theology: Sovereign Grace in Conversion. The conversion of Saul is the New Testament’s clearest portrait of unconditional election and effectual calling. There is nothing in Saul that would attract God’s grace — he is actively persecuting the church, violently opposed to Christ, supremely confident in his own righteousness (Philippians 3:4–6). God chose him anyway. Not because of anything foreseen in him, but according to his own sovereign purpose — to display the fullness of his grace in the most unlikely vessel imaginable. Paul himself will later write that his conversion was designed to be a pattern, “an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life” (1 Timothy 1:16). If God can save Saul of Tarsus, he can save anyone. That is the point. The doctrine of election is not a closed door; it is the foundation of missionary confidence.
9.examples:
Then: A church that had watched Saul drag their brothers and sisters to prison now had to welcome him as a brother. Understandably, they were afraid. It took Barnabas — son of encouragement — to stand between the suspicious church and the new apostle and vouch for the reality of his conversion. The church that had prayed for boldness now needed faith to receive the answer.

Now: No one is beyond the reach of sovereign grace. The person who seems most violently opposed to the gospel may be the one God is about to apprehend. This is not a reason for naivety; it is a reason for prayer — the kind of prayer that believes God can stop any Saul on any road at any time. The church’s task is to be ready, like Ananias, to say “brother” when the moment comes.

10.title: The Gospel to the Gentiles
10.text: <sup>1</sup>At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, <sup>2</sup>a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God. <sup>3</sup>About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, “Cornelius.” <sup>4</sup>And he stared at him in terror and said, “What is it, Lord?” And he said to him, “Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God. <sup>5</sup>And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. <sup>6</sup>He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea.” <sup>7</sup>When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him, <sup>8</sup>and having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa. <sup>9</sup>The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. <sup>10</sup>And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance <sup>11</sup>and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth. <sup>12</sup>In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. <sup>13</sup>And there came a voice to him: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat.” <sup>14</sup>But Peter said, “By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.” <sup>15</sup>And the voice came to him again a second time, “What God has made clean, do not call common.” <sup>16</sup>This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven. <sup>17</sup>Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stood at the gate <sup>18</sup>and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there. <sup>19</sup>And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men are looking for you. <sup>20</sup>Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them.” <sup>21</sup>And Peter went down to the men and said, “I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming?” <sup>22</sup>And they said, “Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man, who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, was directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say.” <sup>23</sup>So he invited them in to be his guests. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him. <sup>24</sup>And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. <sup>25</sup>When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him. <sup>26</sup>But Peter lifted him up, saying, “Stand up; I too am a man.” <sup>27</sup>And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. <sup>28</sup>And he said to them, “You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. <sup>29</sup>So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me.” <sup>30</sup>And Cornelius said, “Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing <sup>31</sup>and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God. <sup>32</sup>Send therefore to Joppa and ask for Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.’ <sup>33</sup>So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord.” <sup>34</sup>So Peter opened his mouth and said: “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, <sup>35</sup>but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him. <sup>36</sup>As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all), <sup>37</sup>you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: <sup>38</sup>how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him. <sup>39</sup>And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, <sup>40</sup>but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear, <sup>41</sup>not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. <sup>42</sup>And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. <sup>43</sup>To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.” <sup>44</sup>While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. <sup>45</sup>And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles. <sup>46</sup>For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared, <sup>47</sup>“Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?” <sup>48</sup>And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.
10.overview:
This is one of the turning points of Acts, so important that Luke tells it twice (again in chapter 11) and Peter retells it at the Jerusalem council (15:7–11). The gospel has reached Samaritans and one Ethiopian; now it reaches Gentiles as Gentiles. Cornelius is a Roman centurion stationed at Caesarea, the Roman capital of Judea, a “God-fearer”: a Gentile who worshipped Israel’s God, prayed at the Jewish hours of prayer and gave generously to Jewish causes, but had not become a Jew by circumcision. In a vision at three in the afternoon an angel tells him that God has noticed his prayers and gifts, and that he should send to Joppa for Simon Peter.

The next day at noon, on a flat rooftop in Joppa, Peter sees a sheet let down from heaven full of animals the law of Moses called unclean, and hears a voice telling him to kill and eat. He refuses, and the voice answers: “What God has made clean, do not call common.” This happens three times. As he puzzles over it, Cornelius’s messengers arrive, and the Spirit tells him to go with them. Peter, who earlier would never have entered a Gentile’s house, goes to Caesarea, finds a house full of Cornelius’s relatives and friends, and declares that God shows no partiality. He preaches Jesus: anointed with the Spirit, doing good and healing, killed on a tree, raised on the third day, appointed judge of the living and the dead, and the one through whom everyone who believes receives forgiveness. While he is still speaking, the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentiles, they speak in tongues and praise God, and Peter’s Jewish companions are astonished. Peter asks who could refuse them water for baptism, and they are baptised in the name of Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–48 — Cornelius and the Gentile Pentecost
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Cornelius, a God-fearing Roman centurion at Caesarea, is told by an angel to send for Peter in Joppa. The next day Peter, praying on a rooftop at noon, sees a sheet full of animals the law called unclean and hears a voice telling him to eat; when he refuses, the voice says three times that he must not call unclean what God has made clean. Cornelius’s messengers arrive, the Spirit tells Peter to go with them, and he travels to Caesarea, where he enters a Gentile home full of people waiting to hear him. Peter declares that God shows no favouritism and accepts people from every nation who fear him. He tells them about Jesus: anointed by the Spirit, doing good and healing, put to death on a cross, raised on the third day, seen by chosen witnesses, appointed judge of all, and the one through whom everyone who believes receives forgiveness. While he is still speaking, the Spirit falls on all the Gentiles listening, to the astonishment of Peter’s Jewish companions, and Peter has them baptised in the name of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Clean and the Unclean, and What the Food Laws Were For

The sheet is full of animals and the argument is about people, and Peter himself makes the translation at verse 28: God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. The food laws had never been about digestion. They were about difference — a daily, three-times-a-day mechanism for keeping Israel visibly distinct from the nations around it, and they worked, which is why a devout Jew could not eat at a Gentile table without the whole arrangement collapsing. Reformed theology has read the vision as the retirement of a shadow rather than the repeal of a word: the separation was always temporary, always pointing forward, and its purpose was fulfilled the moment the dividing wall of hostility came down in Christ (Ephesians 2:14). What is striking is the order in which Peter learned it. He did not reason his way from Christology to table fellowship. He was given a command he found repellent, obeyed it under protest, and worked out the theology afterwards — which is worth remembering by anyone who assumes conviction always precedes obedience.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter needed a vision repeated three times, a direct instruction from the Spirit, three men at the gate and the Spirit falling in front of witnesses before he would accept what he had been told plainly at the ascension. And even then the church argued about it for a chapter and a half. Now: The instinct to take the gospel to people like ourselves is not usually held as a conviction; it is held as an assumption, which is why it survives so much preaching against it. Peter did not have an opinion about Gentiles that could be corrected. He had a lifetime of habit, and it took God three goes.

verseByVerse.quote: At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God.

Meaning first. Acts 10 is the great turning point of the book: the gospel goes to the Gentiles. God prepares both sides: Cornelius, a Roman officer, through an angel; Peter, a Jewish apostle, through a vision. Peter preaches Christ, the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentiles as he did at Pentecost, and they are baptised. Luke tells the story at length, and Peter retells it twice (11:1–18; 15:7–11), because it settles forever that Gentiles are welcomed into God’s people by faith in Christ, without becoming Jews first.

At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius. Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea, built by Herod the Great and named after Caesar Augustus. Pilate lived there; an inscription with his name was found there in 1961.

A centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort. A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers, the backbone of the Roman army. Centurions in the New Testament are consistently portrayed well (Luke 7:2–10; 23:47).

A devout man who feared God with all his household. Key words. A “God-fearer”: a Gentile who worshipped the God of Israel, attended the synagogue, kept some of the law, but was not circumcised. His whole household shared his faith.

Gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God. “The people”: the Jewish people. He was generous to Israel, like the centurion who built a synagogue (Luke 7:5).

In a sentence. In Caesarea lived Cornelius, a centurion of the Italian Cohort, a devout man who with his whole household feared God, gave generously to the people and prayed to God constantly.

On a Tuesday. God sees those who seek him, even outside the church. Pray that he will send them the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea. A centurion commanded a company of about eighty soldiers. “God-fearers” were Gentiles who worshipped Israel’s God without becoming full converts.

parallels.desc: another centurion who loved the Jewish nation

verseByVerse.quote: About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, "Cornelius." And he stared at him in terror and said, "What is it, Lord?" And he said to him, "Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, “Cornelius.” And he stared at him in terror and said, “What is it, Lord?” And he said to him, “Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God.

About the ninth hour of the day. The ESV notes that the ninth hour was about 3 p.m., the hour of afternoon prayer at the temple (3:1). Cornelius was keeping the Jewish hours of prayer.

He saw clearly in a vision an angel of God. Clearly, not a dream.

And he stared at him in terror and said, “What is it, Lord?” The normal reaction to an angel.

Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God. Key words. “Memorial” (mnēmosynon): the word used of the part of the grain offering burned on the altar (Leviticus 2:2). His prayers rose like incense (Psalm 141:2). God had noticed.

What it does not mean. It does not mean his prayers and alms earned salvation. If they had, he wouldn’t need to send for Peter to hear the message by which he would be saved (11:14). God honoured his seeking by sending him the gospel. Those who seek God sincerely will find him, through Christ (Hebrews 11:6; Jeremiah 29:13).

In a sentence. About three in the afternoon he clearly saw an angel of God come in and call his name, and staring in terror he asked what it was, and the angel said his prayers and gifts to the poor had gone up as a memorial before God.

For worship. God remembers every sincere prayer. He answers in his time, and by his gospel.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the ninth hour was about 3 p.m., the hour of afternoon prayer. A “memorial” offering was one that brought the worshipper to God’s remembrance.

parallels.desc: the memorial portion

verseByVerse.quote: "And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea.

And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. Key words. The angel doesn’t preach the gospel. God has entrusted that to people (2 Corinthians 4:7; Romans 10:14). Angels can point the way, but humans must tell the story.

He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea. A precise address, near the sea because tanners needed water.

In a sentence. The angel told him to send men to Joppa to bring Simon called Peter, who was staying with Simon the tanner by the sea.

On a Tuesday. God has given the gospel to people like you to tell. Angels can’t do it for you.

parallels.desc: Simon the tanner

verseByVerse.quote: When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him, and having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him, and having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.

He called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him. His household shared his faith (v. 2). A God-fearing soldier among them.

And having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa. Immediate obedience.

In a sentence. When the angel left, he called two servants and a devout soldier, told them everything, and sent them to Joppa.

For worship. Cornelius obeyed at once. When God speaks, don’t delay.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance

The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city. God’s timing: Peter’s vision comes just as the messengers arrive.

Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. The ESV notes that the sixth hour was about noon. Flat roofs were used for rest and prayer, private and quiet, often with an awning.

And he became hungry. Hunger prepares him for a vision about food.

He fell into a trance. “Trance” (ekstasis): a state in which God communicates directly, as with Paul (22:17).

In a sentence. The next day, as they neared the city, Peter went up on the roof to pray at noon, and became hungry, and while the food was being prepared he fell into a trance.

On a Tuesday. Peter was praying when God spoke. Keep your times of prayer.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the sixth hour was about noon. Flat roofs were used for prayer and rest.

verseByVerse.quote: and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth.

And saw the heavens opened. The vision comes from God.

Something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth. Perhaps like a ship’s sail, familiar by the sea. Four corners: perhaps the four corners of the earth, all nations.

In a sentence. He saw heaven open and something like a large sheet being lowered to earth by its four corners.

For worship. What comes down from heaven is from God. Accept what he gives.

parallels.desc: the heavens were opened

verseByVerse.quote: In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. And there came a voice to him: "Rise, Peter; kill and eat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. And there came a voice to him: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat.”

In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. The sheet held both clean and unclean creatures together, all mixed. The law divided animals into clean and unclean (Leviticus 11; Deuteronomy 14). Jews ate only clean animals, and contact with unclean ones defiled them.

Rise, Peter; kill and eat. Key words. A shocking command to a law-keeping Jew. Not just “eat the clean ones,” but eat from the mixed sheet.

In a sentence. The sheet held all kinds of animals, reptiles and birds, and a voice told Peter to get up, kill and eat.

On a Tuesday. Sometimes God’s word shocks our habits. Listen anyway.
verseByVerse.note: The sheet held both clean and unclean creatures together, all of which Peter is told to eat.

parallels.desc: clean and unclean animals

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said, "By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter said, “By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.”

By no means, Lord. Key words. A contradiction in terms: “no” and “Lord” together. Peter, as ever, contradicts the Lord (Matthew 16:22; John 13:8). Like Ezekiel, who protested against eating defiled food (Ezekiel 4:14).

For I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean. “Common” means ritually unfit, profane. Peter has kept the food laws all his life. Even after Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), he hadn’t grasped it.

In a sentence. Peter replied, “Certainly not, Lord, I have never eaten anything impure or unclean.”

For worship. You can’t say “no” and “Lord” in the same breath for long. Let him be Lord.
verseByVerse.note: “Common” means ritually unfit, profane.

parallels.desc: “I have never defiled myself”

verseByVerse.quote: And the voice came to him again a second time, "What God has made clean, do not call common." This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the voice came to him again a second time, “What God has made clean, do not call common.” This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven.

What God has made clean, do not call common. Key words. God has declared the unclean clean. The food laws, which separated Israel from the nations (Leviticus 20:24–26), are now set aside, because the separation they symbolised is ended in Christ (Ephesians 2:14–15; Colossians 2:16–17). And the deeper meaning, which Peter will soon see: not food, but people (v. 28). Gentiles are not unclean.

This happened three times. Three times, like Peter’s three denials and three restorations. Emphatic. Peter needed it.

And the thing was taken up at once to heaven. It came from God and went back to him.

Where Christians differ: are the food laws binding today? Some groups, such as Seventh-day Adventists and some Messianic Jews, still keep the Old Testament food laws. Verdict: Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19); this vision confirms it; Paul teaches that food is a matter of freedom (Romans 14:14, 20; 1 Timothy 4:3–5). The food laws were shadows fulfilled in Christ. Christians are free to eat anything with thanksgiving, though they should be considerate of the weaker conscience (Romans 14:15).

In a sentence. The voice spoke again, telling him not to call common what God had made clean, and this happened three times before the sheet was taken back up to heaven.

On a Tuesday. Don’t call unclean anyone God has made clean in Christ. Welcome them.

parallels.desc: he declared all foods clean

verseByVerse.quote: Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon's house, stood at the gate and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stood at the gate and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there.

While Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean. He doesn’t yet understand.

Behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius... stood at the gate. Perfect timing. The explanation is knocking at the door.

In a sentence. While Peter was wondering what the vision meant, the men from Cornelius found Simon’s house and stood at the gate, asking if Simon called Peter was staying there.

For worship. God often explains his word by his providence. Watch for the knock at the gate.

verseByVerse.quote: And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, "Behold, three men are looking for you. Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men are looking for you. Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them.”

The Spirit said to him. The Spirit speaks, a person, guiding.

Behold, three men are looking for you. Two servants and a soldier (v. 7).

Accompany them without hesitation. Key words. “Without hesitation” (mēden diakrinomenos): without making a distinction, without doubting. A word that echoes the vision: make no distinction between Jew and Gentile (11:12; 15:9).

For I have sent them. The Spirit sent Gentiles to fetch Peter.

In a sentence. As Peter thought about the vision, the Spirit told him three men were looking for him, and he should go down and go with them without hesitation, for the Spirit had sent them.

On a Tuesday. When the Spirit leads you towards someone different from you, go without hesitation.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter went down to the men and said, "I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming?" And they said, "Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man, who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, was directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Peter went down to the men and said, “I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming?” And they said, “Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man, who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, was directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say.”

I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming? Peter goes down to meet them.

Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man, who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation. His messengers commend him to a Jew: he respects your people.

Was directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say. Key words. “To hear what you have to say”: Cornelius needs Peter’s message to be saved (11:14). Not his prayers, not his alms, but the gospel.

In a sentence. Peter went down and told the men he was the one they sought, and asked why they had come, and they said Cornelius, a righteous, God-fearing centurion respected by all the Jews, had been told by a holy angel to invite Peter to his house to hear what he had to say.

For worship. The world is waiting to hear what you have to say about Christ. Say it.

verseByVerse.quote: So he invited them in to be his guests. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he invited them in to be his guests. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him.

So he invited them in to be his guests. Key words. The first step: Peter gives hospitality to Gentiles. A Jew hosting Gentiles overnight. The vision is already at work.

The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him. Six brothers (11:12): witnesses. Wise, for what was about to happen would be controversial. Joppa to Caesarea was a journey of about 30 miles.

In a sentence. Peter invited them in as guests, and the next day set out with them, along with some believers from Joppa.

On a Tuesday. Hospitality often comes before the gospel. Open your home.
verseByVerse.note: Joppa to Caesarea was a journey of about 30 miles.

parallels.desc: six brothers accompanied me

verseByVerse.quote: And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him.

Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. Key words. He gathered a congregation. Faith expecting, and generous: he wanted his loved ones to hear too.

Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him. “Worshiped” (prosekynēsen): bowed down. Perhaps he thought Peter was a divine messenger.

In a sentence. The next day they reached Caesarea, where Cornelius was waiting with relatives and close friends he had invited, and when Peter came in, Cornelius met him and fell at his feet in worship.

For worship. Gather your family and friends to hear the gospel. Invite them to church.

parallels.desc: “You must not do that”

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter lifted him up, saying, "Stand up; I too am a man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter lifted him up, saying, “Stand up; I too am a man.”

But Peter lifted him up, saying, “Stand up; I too am a man.” Key words. Peter refuses worship, as Paul and Barnabas will (14:14–15), and the angel in Revelation (19:10; 22:8–9). Worship belongs to God alone. Jesus accepted worship (Matthew 14:33; John 20:28); his apostles refused it. That difference shows who Jesus is.

Where Christians differ: veneration of saints and leaders. Some traditions bow before popes, saints or images. Verdict: Peter, whom Rome calls the first pope, refused to let anyone bow before him. No servant of Christ should receive the reverence due to God.

In a sentence. But Peter raised him up, telling him to stand, for he was only a man.

On a Tuesday. Don’t put any Christian leader on a pedestal. They are only men and women. Worship God.

parallels.desc: we also are men, of like nature with you

verseByVerse.quote: And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. And he said to them, "You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. And he said to them, “You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean.

He went in. Key words. Into a Gentile house. A huge step for a Jew.

You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation. The law did not forbid visiting Gentiles, but Jewish custom treated it as defiling. “Unlawful” (athemiton): taboo, against custom. Strict Jews would not enter Gentile homes or eat with Gentiles (John 18:28; Galatians 2:12).

But God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. Key words. Peter has understood the vision. Not food only, but people. No human being is unclean in God’s sight because of race or nation. The wall of division has come down (Ephesians 2:14).

In a sentence. Talking with Cornelius, Peter went in and found many people gathered, and told them that they knew it was against Jewish custom to associate with or visit a Gentile, but God had shown him not to call anyone impure or unclean.

For worship. In Christ, no one is unclean because of race. Tear down your walls.
verseByVerse.note: The law did not forbid visiting Gentiles, but Jewish custom treated a Gentile home as unclean.

verseByVerse.quote: "So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me.

So when I was sent for, I came without objection. Literally “without saying anything against.” A change from “by no means, Lord” (v. 14).

I ask then why you sent for me. Peter wants to hear Cornelius’s story.

In a sentence. Peter said that when he was sent for he came without objection, and asked why they had sent for him.

On a Tuesday. When God calls you to cross a boundary, go without objection.

verseByVerse.quote: And Cornelius said, "Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing and said, 'Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Cornelius said, “Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God.’

Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour. Cornelius retells the story. Luke repeats it to emphasise its importance.

A man stood before me in bright clothing. The angel (v. 3).

Your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God. God heard.

In a sentence. Cornelius said that four days earlier at three in the afternoon, while praying at home, a man in bright clothing stood before him and told him his prayer had been heard and his gifts to the poor remembered by God.

For worship. Tell what God has done for you. Your story can open hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: "Send therefore to Joppa and ask for Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.' So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Send therefore to Joppa and ask for Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.’ So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord.

So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Gratitude.

Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord. Key words. A model congregation. “All here”: they have gathered. “In the presence of God”: they know they are before God. “To hear”: they are ready to listen. “All”: not selectively. “Commanded by the Lord”: they want God’s word, not Peter’s opinions. Every preacher longs for such hearers.

In a sentence. Cornelius said he had sent for Peter at once as the angel told him, thanked him for coming, and said they were all there before God to hear everything the Lord had commanded him.

On a Tuesday. Come to church like this: in God’s presence, ready to hear all he has commanded.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter opened his mouth and said: "Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Peter opened his mouth and said: “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him.

So Peter opened his mouth. A solemn beginning (8:35).

Truly I understand that God shows no partiality. Key words. “Partiality” (prosōpolēmptēs): literally receiving faces, judging by appearance, favouring one person over another. God doesn’t favour Jews over Gentiles (Deuteronomy 10:17; Romans 2:11). Peter now understands what he had always known in theory.

But in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him. Key words. “Acceptable” (dektos): welcome. Nationality is no barrier. God welcomes the one who fears him, from any nation.

Where Christians differ: are sincere seekers saved without the gospel? Inclusivists read this verse to mean that people who fear God and do right in any religion are saved, even without hearing of Christ. Verdict: Cornelius was not yet saved: the angel said Peter would bring a message by which he would be saved (11:14). “Acceptable” means acceptable as a candidate, someone God welcomes to hear the gospel, regardless of nation. The verse removes ethnic barriers, not the need for Christ. Peter goes straight on to preach that forgiveness comes through faith in Jesus (v. 43).

In a sentence. Peter began by saying he now truly understood that God shows no favouritism, but welcomes from every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right.

For worship. God shows no partiality. Neither should you.

parallels.desc: God is not partial

verseByVerse.quote: "As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all),"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all),

As for the word that he sent to Israel. The gospel came first to Israel.

Preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ. Key words. “Peace”: with God, and between Jew and Gentile (Ephesians 2:14–17). Isaiah 52:7: how beautiful are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace.

He is Lord of all. Key words. Peter’s aside is the heart of it. Not Lord of the Jews only, but of all, Jew and Gentile (Romans 10:12). A title the Romans gave to Caesar. Peter gives it to Jesus, in the house of a Roman officer.

In a sentence. Peter said God sent the message to Israel, announcing the good news of peace through Jesus Christ, who is Lord of all.

For worship. Jesus is Lord of all: every nation, every person, every part of your life.

parallels.desc: who publishes peace

verseByVerse.quote: "you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.

You yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee. Peter’s outline of Jesus’ life resembles the shape of Mark’s Gospel: beginning from Galilee, after John’s baptism, through Jesus’ ministry, to his death and resurrection. Early church tradition says Mark wrote down Peter’s preaching.

How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. Key words. At his baptism (Luke 3:22; 4:18). “Anointed”: Christ, Messiah, means the anointed one. The Trinity again: God anointed Jesus with the Spirit.

He went about doing good. A beautiful summary of Jesus’ life.

And healing all who were oppressed by the devil. Jesus’ healings were a war against the devil’s tyranny (Luke 13:16; 1 John 3:8).

For God was with him. The explanation of his power. Peter speaks of his true humanity: a man empowered by the Spirit. Elsewhere Peter calls him Lord of all and judge of all (vv. 36, 42).

In a sentence. Peter reminded them of what happened throughout Judea, starting in Galilee after John’s baptism: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and power, and he went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with him.

On a Tuesday. Go about doing good today, as Jesus did.
verseByVerse.note: Peter’s outline of Jesus’ life resembles the shape of Mark’s Gospel.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me

verseByVerse.quote: "And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear,

And we are witnesses of all that he did. Eyewitness testimony again.

They put him to death by hanging him on a tree. Being hung on a tree was under God’s curse in the law (Deuteronomy 21:23). He bore the curse (Galatians 3:13).

But God raised him on the third day. The resurrection, the heart of the gospel.

And made him to appear. Literally “gave him to become visible.” Real appearances.

In a sentence. Peter said the apostles were witnesses of all Jesus did in Judea and Jerusalem, and though they killed him by hanging him on a tree, God raised him on the third day and made him appear.

For worship. He hung on the tree under the curse, and rose on the third day. That is your gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Being hung on a tree was under God’s curse in the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.

Not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses. Key words. The risen Jesus did not appear to everyone, but to chosen witnesses. Why? Faith comes by hearing their testimony (John 20:29; Romans 10:17). God chose to spread the news by witness, not by spectacle.

Who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. Proof of a real, physical resurrection (Luke 24:41–43; John 21:12–13). Ghosts don’t eat.

In a sentence. He appeared not to all the people, but to witnesses God had chosen beforehand, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.

On a Tuesday. You believe on the testimony of chosen witnesses. Their word is enough.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.

And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. Key words. Jesus is the judge of all (17:31; John 5:22; 2 Timothy 4:1). The gospel includes the warning of judgment. Every person will stand before him.

To him all the prophets bear witness. The whole Old Testament points to Christ (Luke 24:27).

That everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name. Key words. The climax of Peter’s sermon, and the answer to Cornelius’s prayers. “Everyone”: Jew or Gentile. “Who believes in him”: faith alone, not circumcision, not law-keeping, not good works. “Receives forgiveness of sins”: a gift received. “Through his name”: by who he is and what he has done.

Where Christians differ: how are we justified? Some teach that forgiveness comes through faith plus sacraments, or faith plus works. Verdict: Peter says forgiveness is received by everyone who believes, and the Spirit falls before any baptism or work is done (v. 44). This is justification by faith alone, through Christ alone, by grace alone.

In a sentence. Jesus commanded them to preach and testify that he is the one God appointed as judge of the living and the dead, and all the prophets testify that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.

For worship. Everyone who believes in him is forgiven. Everyone. Believe, and rejoice.

verseByVerse.quote: While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles.

While Peter was still saying these things. Key words. God interrupts the sermon. Peter hadn’t even finished. As soon as they heard “everyone who believes receives forgiveness,” they believed, and God sealed it.

The Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. Faith comes by hearing (Romans 10:17), and the Spirit with it (Galatians 3:2).

The believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed. The six Jewish believers from Joppa.

Because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles. “Even on the Gentiles”: unthinkable, but undeniable. God accepted them as they were, uncircumcised.

In a sentence. While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit came on all who heard the message, and the circumcised believers who had come with Peter were astonished that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even on Gentiles.

For worship. The Spirit is poured out on all who believe, whatever their background. Praise God for the Gentile Pentecost.

verseByVerse.quote: For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared,

For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Key words. The same sign as Pentecost (2:4, 11). Visible, undeniable evidence that God had given the same gift to Gentiles as to Jews (11:15–17). The tongues served as proof, at a turning point in the church’s history. “Extolling” (megalynontōn): magnifying, praising. As at Pentecost, they declared the mighty works of God.

Then Peter declared. He sees what this means.

In a sentence. They heard them speaking in tongues and praising God, and Peter said...

For worship. The Spirit’s gift always leads to praise of God. Magnify him today.

verseByVerse.quote: "Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?" And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?” And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.

Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have? Key words. “Withhold” (kōlysai): prevent, the same word as the eunuch’s question (8:36). If God has given the reality, who can refuse the sign? “Just as we have”: no second-class Gentile believers.

And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Baptism follows faith and the Spirit. The order shows that baptism is not what brings the Spirit or forgiveness; it publicly marks what God has done.

Then they asked him to remain for some days. And Peter stayed, eating with Gentiles (11:3). The wall is truly down.

In a sentence. Peter asked whether anyone could refuse water to baptise these people who had received the Spirit just as they had, and ordered them baptised in the name of Jesus Christ, and they asked him to stay a few days.

On a Tuesday. If God has accepted someone, so must you. Welcome every believer as a brother or sister.

10.theology: Election and the Nations. Acts 10 is the fulfilment of the promise to Abraham: “in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed” (Genesis 22:18). The blessing always intended to reach the Gentiles; what Acts 10 shows is the mechanism — the proclamation of Jesus Christ, Lord of all, and the sovereign gift of the Holy Spirit to all who believe. The Gentile mission is not an emergency plan devised when Israel rejected the Messiah. It is the ancient plan of the God who chose Abraham in order to bless the world through him. Peter’s visit to Cornelius is, in the deepest sense, the arrival of what Genesis 12 promised. The God who shows no partiality has always intended a people from every nation. Acts 10 is that intention breaking into history.
10.examples:
