verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed.

And when they had appointed elders for them in every church. Key words. Elders were leaders appointed in each church, as in the synagogue. Plural: a group of elders in every church, not a single pastor (20:17; Philippians 1:1; Titus 1:5). “Appointed” (cheirotonēsantes): possibly by a show of hands, suggesting the congregation took part. Elders are also called overseers (20:28; Titus 1:5–7) and shepherds (1 Peter 5:1–2).

Where Christians differ: church government. Episcopal churches have bishops over many churches; Presbyterians, elders gathered in courts; Congregationalists and Baptists, congregations governed by their own members and elders. Verdict: the New Testament pattern is a plurality of qualified elders in each local church, recognised with the congregation’s involvement, with deacons serving alongside (1 Timothy 3). Elder and bishop (overseer) are the same office in the New Testament. Christ alone is head of the church.

With prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed. Key words. They left them in the Lord’s hands. Missionaries must trust Christ with the churches they plant. The Lord, not Paul, would keep them.

In a sentence. They appointed elders for them in every church, and with prayer and fasting entrusted them to the Lord in whom they had believed.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your elders. And commit those you care for to the Lord; he will keep them better than you can.
verseByVerse.note: Elders were leaders appointed in each church, as in the synagogues.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia. And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia. And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia,

And when they had spoken the word in Perga. They had passed through Perga quickly before (13:13). Now they preach there.

They went down to Attalia. Attalia was the port on the south coast, modern Antalya.

In a sentence. They went through Pisidia to Pamphylia, preached the word in Perga, and went down to Attalia.

For worship. Every stop is an opportunity for the word. Don’t waste yours.
verseByVerse.note: Attalia was the port on the south coast.

verseByVerse.quote: and from there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work that they had fulfilled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and from there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work that they had fulfilled.

And from there they sailed to Antioch. Home to Syrian Antioch, about two years after setting out.

Where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work that they had fulfilled. Key words. They went out committed to God’s grace, and came back having fulfilled the work. Grace sent them, kept them, and finished the work through them.

In a sentence. From there they sailed back to Antioch, where they had been entrusted to God’s grace for the work they had now completed.

For worship. What God’s grace begins, it completes (Philippians 1:6).

verseByVerse.quote: And when they arrived and gathered the church together, they declared all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. And they remained no little time with the disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they arrived and gathered the church together, they declared all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. And they remained no little time with the disciples.

And when they arrived and gathered the church together. They reported to the sending church. Missionaries are accountable to the church that sends them.

They declared all that God had done with them. Key words. Not what they had done, but what God had done with them. The right way to give a missionary report.

And how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. Key words. A door of faith: God opened it (1 Corinthians 16:9; Colossians 4:3). Gentiles could come in through faith alone. This conclusion would soon be challenged (15:1).

And they remained no little time with the disciples. Rest and fellowship.

In a sentence. When they arrived, they gathered the church and reported all that God had done through them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles, and they stayed there a long time with the disciples.

On a Tuesday. When you tell of God’s work, give him the credit: what God has done.

parallels.desc: a wide door for effective work

14.theology: Suffering as the Path of the Kingdom. Acts 14:22 is the New Testament’s clearest statement that suffering is the appointed means by which the people of God enter the kingdom. This is not peripheral; it is structural. The cross was not a detour on the way to the resurrection; it was the way. And the church that follows a crucified Lord is called to the same road. Paul writes later that he fills up in his flesh “what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body” (Colossians 1:24) — not that Christ’s atoning work was incomplete, but that the suffering of Christ is reproduced in his body, the church, as the gospel goes forth into the world. The church that suffers for the name is the church that looks most like its Lord. And it is the church that the watching world cannot ultimately explain away.
14.examples:
Then: Paul, stoned and left for dead outside Lystra, rising and walking back into the city, going on to Derbe the next morning. Returning through Lystra and Iconium and Antioch — the cities that had tried to kill him — to strengthen the believers he left behind. Appointing elders, committing them to God with prayer and fasting, and sailing home to report everything God had done. This is what faithful looks like.

Now: The Western church has largely lost the theology of suffering. We expect the Christian life to be comfortable, and when it is not, we assume something has gone wrong. Acts 14 says the opposite: tribulation is the appointed road, and the God who walked it first walks it with his people. The suffering church is not the failing church; it is often the most faithful church — and, in God’s strange economy, the most fruitful.

15.title: The Jerusalem Council
15.text: <sup>1</sup>But some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” <sup>2</sup>And after Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them, Paul and Barnabas and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders about this question. <sup>3</sup>So, being sent on their way by the church, they passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles, and brought great joy to all the brothers. <sup>4</sup>When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and the elders, and they declared all that God had done with them. <sup>5</sup>But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees rose up and said, “It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses.” <sup>6</sup>The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. <sup>7</sup>And after there had been much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe. <sup>8</sup>And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, <sup>9</sup>and he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith. <sup>10</sup>Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? <sup>11</sup>But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.” <sup>12</sup>And all the assembly fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul as they related what signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles. <sup>13</sup>After they finished speaking, James replied, “Brothers, listen to me. <sup>14</sup>Simeon has related how God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name. <sup>15</sup>And with this the words of the prophets agree, just as it is written, <sup>16</sup>‘After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen; I will rebuild its ruins, and I will restore it, <sup>17</sup>that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who makes these things <sup>18</sup>known from of old.’ <sup>19</sup>Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God, <sup>20</sup>but should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols, and from sexual immorality, and from what has been strangled, and from blood. <sup>21</sup>For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him, for he is read every Sabbath in the synagogues.” <sup>22</sup>Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They sent Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers, <sup>23</sup>with the following letter: “The brothers, both the apostles and the elders, to the brothers who are of the Gentiles in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia, greetings. <sup>24</sup>Since we have heard that some persons have gone out from us and troubled you with words, unsettling your minds, although we gave them no instructions, <sup>25</sup>it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul, <sup>26</sup>men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>27</sup>We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who themselves will tell you the same things by word of mouth. <sup>28</sup>For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these requirements: <sup>29</sup>that you abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.” <sup>30</sup>So when they were sent off, they went down to Antioch, and having gathered the congregation together, they delivered the letter. <sup>31</sup>And when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement. <sup>32</sup>And Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets, encouraged and strengthened the brothers with many words. <sup>33</sup>And after they had spent some time, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them. <sup>35</sup>But Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also. <sup>36</sup>And after some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are.” <sup>37</sup>Now Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark. <sup>38</sup>But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work. <sup>39</sup>And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus, <sup>40</sup>but Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord. <sup>41</sup>And he went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.
15.overview:
The success of the Gentile mission raises the most important question the early church faced. Some Jewish believers from Judea arrive in Antioch teaching that Gentile converts cannot be saved unless they are circumcised and keep the law of Moses: in effect, Gentiles must become Jews to become Christians. This was not an odd idea. Circumcision was the covenant sign God gave Abraham, and for centuries any Gentile who wanted to join God’s people had done exactly that. Paul and Barnabas dispute it fiercely, and the church sends them to Jerusalem to settle it with the apostles and elders.

At the council, believers from the Pharisee party insist on circumcision. Peter reminds everyone how God gave the Spirit to Cornelius’s household, cleansing their hearts by faith, and asks why they would put on Gentiles a yoke that neither they nor their ancestors could bear, since Jews and Gentiles alike are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus. Paul and Barnabas tell of the signs God did among the Gentiles. Then James, the Lord’s brother and leader of the Jerusalem church, shows from the prophet Amos that God always planned to gather Gentiles to rebuild David’s fallen house, and proposes that Gentile believers should not be burdened with the law, but asked to avoid food offered to idols, sexual immorality, the meat of strangled animals and blood, practices especially offensive to Jews, so that Jewish and Gentile believers could share fellowship. A letter is sent with Judas and Silas, and Antioch rejoices. The chapter ends with a painful disagreement: Paul and Barnabas part company over whether to take John Mark on a second journey, so Barnabas sails with Mark to Cyprus and Paul sets out with Silas.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Teachers from Judea tell the Gentile believers in Antioch that they cannot be saved without circumcision and the law of Moses. Paul and Barnabas oppose them, and the church sends them to Jerusalem. There believers from the Pharisee party press the same demand. After long debate Peter reminds the council that God gave the Spirit to Gentiles who believed, making no distinction and cleansing their hearts by faith, and that Jews and Gentiles alike are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus, not by a yoke no one could carry. Paul and Barnabas describe God’s signs among the Gentiles. James then shows from Amos that God planned to gather Gentiles into the restored house of David, and proposes that they be asked only to avoid idol food, sexual immorality, strangled meat and blood. The apostles, elders and whole church agree, and send a letter with Judas and Silas declaring that it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to them to lay no greater burden on the Gentiles. The church in Antioch rejoices.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by Faith Alone — the Council's Theological Verdict

Peter's speech in vv. 8–11 is the clearest statement of justification by faith alone in the book of Acts: 'God made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith... we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.' The Gentiles are saved the same way the Jews are — by grace through faith, not by law observance. This is the verdict that Paul will develop in Galatians and Romans. The Jerusalem Council is the communal confirmation of what the Spirit had demonstrated in Cornelius's house.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Jerusalem Council produced a letter of pastoral decision rather than a theological treatise — practical guidance that allowed Jew and Gentile to live together in one community. Now: The church continues to face questions about what is required for full membership in the people of God. The council's method — testimony, Scripture, deliberation, pastoral wisdom — remains the model for ecclesial discernment on divisive questions.

verseByVerse.quote: But some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, "Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved." And after Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them, Paul and Barnabas and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders about this question.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” And after Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them, Paul and Barnabas and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders about this question.

Meaning first. Acts 15 is the centre of the book, and one of the most important chapters in the history of the church. The question is: must Gentiles become Jews to be saved? Must they be circumcised and keep the law of Moses? The Jerusalem council answers: no. We are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, Jew and Gentile alike, by faith. Gentile believers are asked only to avoid certain practices that would offend Jewish believers and make fellowship impossible. The gospel of grace is preserved, and the church stays one. Paul’s letter to the Galatians fights the same battle.

But some men came down from Judea. Probably those mentioned in Galatians 2:12, claiming to come from James, though they had no instructions from him (v. 24).

Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved. Key words. Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham (Genesis 17); the question was whether Gentile believers must receive it, and with it keep the whole law (Galatians 5:3). Notice what is at stake: “you cannot be saved.” Not a matter of custom, but of salvation. Christ plus circumcision. Paul called it a different gospel (Galatians 1:6–9).

No small dissension and debate. Understatement. Paul would not give in for a moment (Galatians 2:5).

Paul and Barnabas and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders about this question. The church seeks unity through consultation, not separation.

In a sentence. Some men came from Judea teaching that unless Gentiles were circumcised according to Moses’ custom they could not be saved, and after fierce debate with them, Paul, Barnabas and others were appointed to go to Jerusalem to the apostles and elders about this question.

On a Tuesday. Watch for “Jesus plus” teaching: Jesus plus rules, rituals, or works. It is another gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham; the question was whether Gentiles must become Jews to be saved. This meeting in Jerusalem, about AD 49, is often called the Jerusalem Council.

parallels.desc: Paul’s account of a Jerusalem meeting

verseByVerse.quote: "So, being sent on their way by the church, they passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles, and brought great joy to all the brothers. When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and the elders, and they declared all that God had done with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, being sent on their way by the church, they passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles, and brought great joy to all the brothers. When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and the elders, and they declared all that God had done with them.

Being sent on their way by the church. With the church’s support.

They passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles, and brought great joy to all the brothers. Key words. Churches founded by the scattered believers (8:4; 11:19). The Samaritans, once outsiders themselves, rejoice at Gentiles coming in.

When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed. Warmly.

And they declared all that God had done with them. Again, what God had done (14:27).

In a sentence. Sent on their way by the church, they travelled through Phoenicia and Samaria telling about the conversion of the Gentiles, bringing great joy to all the believers, and in Jerusalem they were welcomed by the church, apostles and elders, and reported everything God had done through them.

For worship. News of conversions should bring joy. Share it.

verseByVerse.quote: "But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees rose up and said, 'It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees rose up and said, “It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses.”

But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees. Key words. Believers. Genuine Christians, who still held a Pharisee’s view of the law. Paul was a Pharisee too (23:6; Philippians 3:5), but had learned better.

It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses. “Necessary” (dei): required. Their view: Gentiles must become Jews to belong to God’s people. The whole law, not only circumcision.

In a sentence. But some believers from the party of the Pharisees stood up and said that Gentiles must be circumcised and ordered to keep the law of Moses.

On a Tuesday. True believers can hold wrong views. Correct them with Scripture, patiently.

parallels.desc: as to the law, a Pharisee

verseByVerse.quote: The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. And after there had been much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, "Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. And after there had been much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe.

The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. The first church council. The whole church was involved (vv. 12, 22).

And after there had been much debate. Open, honest discussion. Not a decree from above.

Peter stood up. His last appearance in Acts.

God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe. Key words. Cornelius, about ten years earlier (chapter 10). God himself chose to bring Gentiles in through Peter. Hearing and believing: that is how Gentiles came in. Nothing was said about circumcision.

In a sentence. The apostles and elders met to consider the matter, and after much debate Peter stood up and reminded them that early on God chose him so that the Gentiles would hear the gospel from him and believe.

For worship. The gospel is heard and believed. That is how anyone enters God’s family.

verseByVerse.quote: "And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, and he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, and he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith.

And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us. Key words. God knows hearts (1:24). He saw their faith and gave them the Spirit, the proof that he had accepted them, before any circumcision.

And he made no distinction between us and them. No first and second class.

Having cleansed their hearts by faith. Key words. Not by circumcision, not by washings, not by the law, but by faith. The heart is the place that needs cleansing, and faith is the means (10:15; Hebrews 9:14). Outward rituals can’t cleanse the heart.

In a sentence. Peter said God, who knows the heart, showed he accepted the Gentiles by giving them the Holy Spirit as he did the apostles, making no distinction between them, for he cleansed their hearts by faith.

On a Tuesday. Your heart is cleansed by faith in Christ, not by religious performance.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.

Why are you putting God to the test. To demand more than God has demanded is to challenge him, to question his decision.

By placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? Key words. A yoke joined animals together for work; teachers spoke of the law as a yoke to be taken up. Peter says it was a yoke no one could bear: no one kept the law perfectly (Galatians 3:10; James 2:10). Jesus offers an easy yoke (Matthew 11:29–30). To require the law for salvation is to put a crushing weight on believers.

But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will. Key words. The great conclusion. Peter turns it round: not “they will be saved as we are, by becoming Jews,” but “we Jews are saved as they are, by grace.” Grace alone, through the Lord Jesus alone. The same way for everyone.

In a sentence. Peter asked why they were testing God by putting on the disciples a yoke neither they nor their fathers could carry, for they believed they were saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as the Gentiles were.

For worship. We are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus. All of us, the same way. Rest in grace.
verseByVerse.note: A yoke joined animals together for work; teachers spoke of the “yoke” of the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "And all the assembly fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul as they related what signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles. After they finished speaking, James replied, 'Brothers, listen to me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all the assembly fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul as they related what signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles. After they finished speaking, James replied, “Brothers, listen to me.

And all the assembly fell silent. Peter’s words settled the debate.

They listened to Barnabas and Paul as they related what signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles. Evidence: God had confirmed the Gentile mission with signs. Barnabas named first, as the trusted figure in Jerusalem.

James replied. This James is the Lord’s brother, leader of the Jerusalem church (12:17). A man known for strict law-keeping, respected by conservative Jewish believers. His judgment would carry weight with them.

In a sentence. The whole assembly fell silent and listened as Barnabas and Paul described the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them, and when they finished, James spoke up.

On a Tuesday. In disputes, listen to the evidence of what God is doing. Then let Scripture decide.
verseByVerse.note: This James is the Lord’s brother, leader of the Jerusalem church.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Simeon has related how God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon has related how God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name.

Simeon has related. Simeon is the Hebrew form of Simon (Peter). James uses the old Jewish name (2 Peter 1:1).

How God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name. Key words. “A people for his name”: a phrase used of Israel (Deuteronomy 14:2). Now God takes a people from the Gentiles too. The church is not a Gentile replacement for Israel, but God’s one people, from Jews and Gentiles, the Israel of God (Galatians 6:16).

In a sentence. James said Simeon had told how God first visited the Gentiles to take from them a people for his name.

For worship. God has taken a people for his name from every nation. You are one of them. Bear his name well.
verseByVerse.note: Simeon is the Hebrew form of Simon (Peter).

verseByVerse.quote: "And with this the words of the prophets agree, just as it is written, "'After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen; I will rebuild its ruins, and I will restore it,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And with this the words of the prophets agree, just as it is written, ‘After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen; I will rebuild its ruins, and I will restore it,

And with this the words of the prophets agree. Key words. Experience is confirmed by Scripture. James doesn’t rely only on the stories; he goes to the Bible. Scripture has the final word.

After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen. James quotes Amos in its Greek form. “The tent of David” is David’s dynasty and kingdom, fallen into ruin (Amos 9:11). God promised to restore it.

I will rebuild its ruins, and I will restore it. James says this is being fulfilled now: in the resurrection and enthronement of Jesus, David’s son (2:30–36; 13:34), and in the gathering of the Gentiles into his kingdom.

Where Christians differ: when is David’s tent rebuilt? Dispensationalists see the rebuilding of David’s tent as a future millennial kingdom for Israel, after the church age. Verdict: James says the conversion of the Gentiles agrees with Amos now. David’s fallen tent is rebuilt in the risen Christ reigning on David’s throne, and in his church of Jews and Gentiles. The promise is fulfilled in the gospel age. This is the amillennial reading, which follows the apostles’ own use of the prophets.

In a sentence. James said the prophets agree, as Amos wrote that afterwards God would return and rebuild the fallen tent of David, rebuilding its ruins and restoring it.

On a Tuesday. Test every claim by Scripture. Experience must agree with the word.
verseByVerse.note: James quotes Amos in its Greek form. “The tent of David” is David’s fallen royal house.

parallels.desc: I will raise up the booth of David that is fallen

verseByVerse.quote: "'that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who makes these things'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who makes these things

That the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord. Key words. The purpose of rebuilding David’s tent: that the rest of humanity might seek the Lord. The Hebrew of Amos reads “that they may possess the remnant of Edom,” and the Greek translation, which James uses, read the Hebrew letters slightly differently as “mankind.” Either way, the nations are brought under the rule of David’s son.

And all the Gentiles who are called by my name. Key words. Gentiles called by God’s name: belonging to him, as Gentiles, without first becoming Jews. This is the decisive point. Amos doesn’t say the Gentiles will become Jews; he says Gentiles will bear God’s name.

Says the Lord, who makes these things. God does it.

In a sentence. Amos says this was so that the rest of humanity, all the Gentiles called by God’s name, would seek the Lord, says the Lord who does these things.

For worship. God’s name is on Gentiles who believe. Wear it with gratitude.

parallels.desc: all the nations who are called by my name

verseByVerse.quote: "'known from of old.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
known from of old.

Known from of old. Key words. God has always planned this, from eternity (Isaiah 45:21; Ephesians 3:9–11). The inclusion of the Gentiles was not plan B, but God’s purpose all along, made known to Abraham (Genesis 12:3).

In a sentence. These things were known from long ago.

For worship. God planned your salvation from of old. Nothing about it is an afterthought.

parallels.desc: who told this long ago?

verseByVerse.quote: "'Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God, but should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols, and from sexual immorality, and from what has been strangled, and from blood.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God, but should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols, and from sexual immorality, and from what has been strangled, and from blood.

Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God. Key words. The decision: no circumcision, no burden of the law. “Trouble” (parenochlein): pile on difficulties. Gentiles are saved as Gentiles.

But should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols, and from sexual immorality, and from what has been strangled, and from blood. The four requirements probably echo rules the law gave for foreigners living among Israel (Leviticus 17–18). Food offered to idols; sexual immorality (perhaps including marriages within forbidden degrees, Leviticus 18); meat from animals strangled rather than drained of blood; and eating blood (Genesis 9:4). These would deeply offend Jewish believers and make table fellowship impossible.

Where Christians differ: are these rules binding today? Some groups hold that Christians must still avoid blood, for example in black pudding, or even (Jehovah’s Witnesses) blood transfusions. Verdict: these were not conditions of salvation (that was settled in v. 11), but practical rules for fellowship between Jewish and Gentile believers at that time. Paul later teaches that food is a matter of conscience and love (Romans 14; 1 Corinthians 8–10). The rule against sexual immorality is permanent moral law; the food rules applied the principle of not offending a brother. Blood transfusions have nothing to do with eating blood.

In a sentence. James gave his judgment that they should not burden the Gentiles who turn to God, but write telling them to avoid things polluted by idols, sexual immorality, the meat of strangled animals, and blood.

On a Tuesday. Don’t add burdens to the gospel. But be willing to give up freedoms for the sake of fellowship.
verseByVerse.note: The four requirements probably echo rules the law gave for foreigners living in Israel (Lev 17–18), and would let Jewish and Gentile believers eat together.

parallels.desc: sacrifices, blood, and what dies of itself
sexual relations

verseByVerse.quote: "'For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him, for he is read every Sabbath in the synagogues.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him, for he is read every Sabbath in the synagogues.

For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him. Key words. The reason for the requirements: Jews lived in every city and heard the law every week. Gentile believers should be sensitive to them, so as not to put stumbling blocks in their way to Christ, and so that Jewish and Gentile believers could eat together.

For he is read every Sabbath in the synagogues. The Jewish community would be watching how Gentile Christians lived.

In a sentence. For Moses has been preached in every city from ancient times and read in the synagogues every Sabbath.

For worship. Live so as not to put stumbling blocks in front of others. Love limits liberty.

verseByVerse.quote: Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They sent Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers, with the following letter: "The brothers, both the apostles and the elders, to the brothers who are of the Gentiles in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia, greetings."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They sent Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers, with the following letter: “The brothers, both the apostles and the elders, to the brothers who are of the Gentiles in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia, greetings.

Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church. Key words. Agreement: leaders and congregation together. Unity, after great debate.

To choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. Messengers from Jerusalem would confirm the letter was genuine, so that no one could say Paul made it up.

They sent Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas. Silas is the Silvanus of Paul’s letters; he became Paul’s travelling companion (v. 40; 2 Corinthians 1:19; 1 Thessalonians 1:1) and helped Peter write his first letter (1 Peter 5:12). A Roman citizen (16:37).

The brothers, both the apostles and the elders, to the brothers who are of the Gentiles. “Brothers” to “brothers”: Jewish and Gentile believers are one family.

In a sentence. The apostles, elders and whole church decided to send chosen men, Judas Barsabbas and Silas, leaders among the brothers, to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas, carrying a letter from the apostles and elders to the Gentile believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia.

On a Tuesday. Call every believer “brother” or “sister.” In Christ, we are family.
verseByVerse.note: Silas is the Silvanus of Paul’s letters; he became Paul’s travelling companion.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Since we have heard that some persons have gone out from us and troubled you with words, unsettling your minds, although we gave them no instructions, it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we have heard that some persons have gone out from us and troubled you with words, unsettling your minds, although we gave them no instructions, it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,

Some persons have gone out from us and troubled you with words, unsettling your minds. “Unsettling” (anaskeuazontes): turning upside down, as in plundering a house. False teaching wreaks havoc.

Although we gave them no instructions. Key words. The apostles disown the false teachers. They had no authority from Jerusalem.

Having come to one accord. Unity of mind.

With our beloved Barnabas and Paul. A public endorsement of Paul and Barnabas, against those who questioned them.

In a sentence. The letter said that since some men from Jerusalem had troubled them and unsettled their minds without any authority, the apostles and elders had agreed to choose men and send them with their dear friends Barnabas and Paul.

For worship. False teaching unsettles minds. The truth of grace brings peace.

parallels.desc: some who trouble you

verseByVerse.quote: "'men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who themselves will tell you the same things by word of mouth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who themselves will tell you the same things by word of mouth.

Men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. “Risked” (paradedōkosi): handed over, given up their lives. The stoning at Lystra (14:19). Their suffering proved their sincerity, unlike the troublemakers.

Judas and Silas, who themselves will tell you the same things by word of mouth. Two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15).

In a sentence. Paul and Barnabas had risked their lives for the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, and Judas and Silas would confirm the same things in person.

On a Tuesday. Honour those who have suffered for Christ. Their scars are credentials.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these requirements: that you abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these requirements: that you abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.

For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us. Key words. A remarkable phrase. The Spirit led the council through Scripture, through what God had done, and through the agreement of the church. The Spirit first, then us.

To lay on you no greater burden than these requirements. “No greater burden”: the burden of the law is lifted.

If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Not “you will be saved,” but “you will do well.” Advice for fellowship, not a condition of salvation.

Where Christians differ: the authority of church councils. Some see this council as the model for later councils whose decisions bind the church infallibly. Verdict: this council included apostles, and its decision became Scripture. Later councils have no such authority. They are valuable and to be respected when they agree with Scripture, as Nicaea and Chalcedon do, but they can err (Westminster Confession 31.4). Scripture alone is the final authority. This is sola Scriptura.

In a sentence. The letter said it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to them to put no greater burden on them than to avoid food sacrificed to idols, blood, strangled meat and sexual immorality, and they would do well to keep from these.

For worship. The Spirit lifts the yoke of the law from your neck. Live freely, and lovingly.

verseByVerse.quote: "So when they were sent off, they went down to Antioch, and having gathered the congregation together, they delivered the letter. And when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when they were sent off, they went down to Antioch, and having gathered the congregation together, they delivered the letter. And when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement.

Having gathered the congregation together, they delivered the letter. Read publicly to the whole church.

And when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement. Key words. The Gentile believers were relieved and joyful. They were saved by grace, as they were. The gospel of grace brings joy; legalism brings fear.

In a sentence. The messengers went to Antioch, gathered the church and delivered the letter, and when they read it, they rejoiced at its encouragement.

For worship. Rejoice: you are saved by grace, without the yoke of the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets, encouraged and strengthened the brothers with many words. And after they had spent some time, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets, encouraged and strengthened the brothers with many words. And after they had spent some time, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them.

And Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets, encouraged and strengthened the brothers with many words. Prophets here encourage and strengthen, as Paul describes (1 Corinthians 14:3).

They were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them. Peace restored.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 34: that it seemed good to Silas to remain there. It is probably a later addition to explain why Silas is in Antioch in v. 40. Silas may have gone back to Jerusalem and later returned, or stayed.

In a sentence. Judas and Silas, being prophets themselves, encouraged and strengthened the believers with many words, and after some time were sent back in peace to those who had sent them.

On a Tuesday. Use your words to encourage and strengthen others today.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 34: “But it seemed good to Silas to remain there.”

verseByVerse.quote: But Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also.

Teaching and preaching the word of the Lord. Back to the main work.

With many others also. Key words. The ministry of the word was shared by many. A healthy church has many teachers.

In a sentence. Paul and Barnabas stayed in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord with many others.

For worship. The word of the Lord is the heart of church life. Give yourself to it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–41 — The Parting of Paul and Barnabas
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some time later Paul suggested to Barnabas that they go back and visit the believers in every town where they had preached, to see how they were doing. Barnabas wanted to take John, also called Mark, but Paul thought it unwise to take someone who had deserted them in Pamphylia and had not continued in the work. They had such a sharp disagreement that they parted company. Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus, while Paul chose Silas and left, commended by the believers to the grace of the Lord. He went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.
verseByVerse.theology:
God's Sovereignty Over Human Conflict

Reformed theology sees in the Paul-Barnabas conflict the characteristic pattern of God's providence: working through human failure and disagreement to accomplish more than perfect human unity might have achieved. The separation produces two missionary teams instead of one. John Mark, the subject of the dispute, will prove his worth — Paul himself will later commend him (2 Timothy 4:11; Colossians 4:10). God does not waste the failures of his servants; he works through them, around them, and despite them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus — his home, the place that knows him — to restore the man he believes in. Paul took Silas through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches. Both were faithful; both bore fruit. Now: The church's disagreements, when they do not touch the gospel itself, can produce multiplication rather than division if those who disagree remain committed to the mission rather than to winning the argument.

verseByVerse.quote: "And after some days Paul said to Barnabas, 'Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are.' Now Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And after some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are.” Now Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark.

Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are. Key words. Pastoral concern. Paul cared for the churches he planted (2 Corinthians 11:28). Planting is not enough; we must nurture.

Now Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark. His cousin, who had turned back (13:13). Barnabas, the encourager, wanted to give him a second chance.

In a sentence. Some time later Paul suggested to Barnabas that they go back and visit the believers in every city where they had preached, to see how they were doing, and Barnabas wanted to take John Mark.

On a Tuesday. Who did you help come to faith? Check on them. See how they are.

parallels.desc: Mark the cousin of Barnabas

verseByVerse.quote: "But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work.

But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia. Key words. “Withdrawn” (apostanta): deserted, fallen away. Paul saw it as abandoning the work. He needed reliable companions for dangerous journeys. Both men had a point: Barnabas saw a person to restore; Paul saw a mission to protect.

In a sentence. But Paul did not think it wise to take one who had deserted them in Pamphylia and not continued in the work.

For worship. Faithfulness matters in God’s work. But so does mercy for those who failed.

verseByVerse.quote: "And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus, but Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus, but Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord.

And there arose a sharp disagreement. Key words. “Sharp disagreement” (paroxysmos): irritation, provocation. The word gives us “paroxysm.” Luke doesn’t hide the conflict between two godly men. Christians, even apostles, can disagree strongly. Scripture doesn’t say who was right.

So that they separated from each other. A sad parting after years together. But God used it: two missionary teams instead of one.

Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus. Barnabas’s last appearance in Acts. His investment in Mark paid off: Mark became useful to Paul (2 Timothy 4:11) and wrote a Gospel. Paul and Mark were later reconciled (Colossians 4:10; Philemon 24). Paul spoke well of Barnabas later (1 Corinthians 9:6).

But Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord. The church sent Paul with its blessing.

In a sentence. Their disagreement was so sharp that they parted: Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus, while Paul chose Silas and left, commended by the believers to the grace of the Lord.

On a Tuesday. If you have had a sharp disagreement with a fellow believer, seek reconciliation, as Paul and Mark did in the end.
verseByVerse.note: Paul and Mark were later reconciled.

parallels.desc: get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me

verseByVerse.quote: "And he went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.

And he went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches. Key words. Syria and Cilicia, Paul’s home region, where he had worked during his hidden years (Galatians 1:21). The letter of the council was addressed to them (v. 23). Strengthening churches: the work of a pastor and apostle. The second missionary journey begins.

In a sentence. Paul travelled through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.

For worship. Strengthen your church today with a word of encouragement, a prayer, a helping hand.

15.theology: Justification by Grace Alone through Faith Alone. Acts 15 is the original council on justification. Peter’s summary — “we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will” — is the thesis of the Reformation stated by an apostle. The Judaizers were not wicked men; they were sincere believers who thought obedience to the law was necessary for salvation. But sincerity does not make a false gospel true. The council’s verdict is decisive and irreversible: the Gentiles are saved through grace, and so are the Jews. The law cannot save. It never could. The law was given to demonstrate the need for grace, not to provide an alternative to it. The cross of Christ is sufficient, complete, and alone — and any addition to it, however well-intentioned, is a subtraction from it.
15.examples:
Then: A church divided over the most fundamental question imaginable: what must a person do to be saved? The answer came not from compromise but from clarity, grounded in Scripture (James’s citation of Amos) and confirmed by experience (Peter’s witness to Cornelius, Barnabas and Paul’s report from the Gentile mission). The church that settles this question rightly can face every other challenge. The church that gets it wrong has nothing left to offer.

Now: The Judaizer error never stays buried. It reappears in every generation dressed in different clothes: the idea that grace plus something — baptism, church membership, moral effort, liturgical compliance — constitutes salvation. The Jerusalem Council’s answer is permanent and non-negotiable: the grace of the Lord Jesus alone. The church’s task in every generation is to say it clearly, defend it stubbornly, and live it joyfully.

16.title: Into Macedonia
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul came also to Derbe and to Lystra. A disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek. <sup>2</sup>He was well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium. <sup>3</sup>Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek. <sup>4</sup>As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered to them for observance the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem. <sup>5</sup>So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily. <sup>6</sup>And they went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. <sup>7</sup>And when they had come up to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them. <sup>8</sup>So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas. <sup>9</sup>And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him and saying, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” <sup>10</sup>And when Paul had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them. <sup>11</sup>So, setting sail from Troas, we made a direct voyage to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis, <sup>12</sup>and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. We remained in this city some days. <sup>13</sup>And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together. <sup>14</sup>One who heard us was a woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. <sup>15</sup>And after she was baptized, and her household as well, she urged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay.” And she prevailed upon us. <sup>16</sup>As we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a slave girl who had a spirit of divination and brought her owners much gain by fortune-telling. <sup>17</sup>She followed Paul and us, crying out, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation.” <sup>18</sup>And this she kept doing for many days. Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.” And it came out that very hour. <sup>19</sup>But when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers. <sup>20</sup>And when they had brought them to the magistrates, they said, “These men are Jews, and they are disturbing our city. <sup>21</sup>They advocate customs that are not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice.” <sup>22</sup>The crowd joined in attacking them, and the magistrates tore the garments off them and gave orders to beat them with rods. <sup>23</sup>And when they had inflicted many blows upon them, they threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to keep them safely. <sup>24</sup>Having received this order, he put them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks. <sup>25</sup>About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them, <sup>26</sup>and suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. And immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were unfastened. <sup>27</sup>When the jailer woke and saw that the prison doors were open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. <sup>28</sup>But Paul cried with a loud voice, “Do not harm yourself, for we are all here.” <sup>29</sup>And the jailer called for lights and rushed in, and trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas. <sup>30</sup>Then he brought them out and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” <sup>31</sup>And they said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.” <sup>32</sup>And they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house. <sup>33</sup>And he took them the same hour of the night and washed their wounds, and he was baptized at once, he and all his family. <sup>34</sup>Then he brought them up into his house and set food before them. And he rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God. <sup>35</sup>But when it was day, the magistrates sent the police, saying, “Let those men go.” <sup>36</sup>And the jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, “The magistrates have sent to let you go. Therefore come out now and go in peace.” <sup>37</sup>But Paul said to them, “They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens, and have thrown us into prison; and do they now throw us out secretly? No! Let them come themselves and take us out.” <sup>38</sup>The police reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens. <sup>39</sup>So they came and apologized to them. And they took them out and asked them to leave the city. <sup>40</sup>So they went out of the prison and visited Lydia. And when they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed.
16.overview:
Paul’s second journey begins by revisiting the churches of the first. At Lystra he recruits Timothy, a young believer with a Jewish mother and Greek father, and circumcises him so that his ministry among Jews will not be hindered. Then the Spirit repeatedly blocks their plans: they are kept from preaching in the province of Asia and stopped from entering Bithynia, until at Troas, on the Aegean coast, Paul sees a vision of a man of Macedonia begging, “Come over and help us.” Here Luke slips into “we”: he has joined the team. They cross into Europe and go to Philippi, a Roman colony settled with army veterans, proud of its Roman status, where there were too few Jews even for a synagogue. By the river on the Sabbath they find women praying, and the Lord opens the heart of Lydia, a businesswoman who traded in expensive purple cloth, who is baptised with her household and opens her home to them.

Then trouble. Paul casts a spirit of divination out of a slave girl whose fortune-telling made money for her owners, who drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates, accusing them, as Jews, of disturbing the city with un-Roman customs. They are stripped, beaten with rods and put in the stocks in the inner prison. At midnight, as they pray and sing hymns, an earthquake opens the doors and loosens everyone’s chains. The jailer, about to kill himself, cries out, “What must I do to be saved?” and is told, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.” He washes their wounds, he and his household are baptised, and he rejoices that he has come to believe in God. In the morning, when the magistrates order their release, Paul reveals that they are Roman citizens, beaten without trial, and insists that the officials come and escort them out, protecting the young church before he leaves.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Timothy, the Macedonian Call, and Lydia
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Lystra Paul found a disciple named Timothy, son of a Jewish believer and a Greek father, well spoken of by the believers there and in Iconium. Paul wanted to take him on the journey, so he circumcised him because of the Jews in the area, who all knew his father was Greek. As they travelled from town to town, they delivered the decisions of the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, and the churches were strengthened in faith and grew daily in numbers. They travelled through Phrygia and Galatia, having been kept by the Holy Spirit from preaching the word in the province of Asia. When they reached the border of Mysia and tried to enter Bithynia, the Spirit of Jesus would not allow them, so they passed by Mysia and went down to Troas. During the night Paul had a vision of a man of Macedonia standing and begging him to come over and help them. After the vision, Luke writes, we got ready at once to leave for Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them. From Troas we sailed straight to Samothrace, the next day to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi, a Roman colony and leading city of that district of Macedonia, and stayed there several days. On the Sabbath we went outside the city gate to the river, where we expected to find a place of prayer, and sat down to speak to the women who had gathered. One of them was Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira, a worshipper of God. The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message. When she and her household had been baptised, she invited us to stay at her house if we considered her a believer in the Lord, and she persuaded us.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit's Direction of Mission

The second missionary journey is notable for the Spirit's specific prevention and redirection: 'they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia... the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them' to go to Bithynia. The door to Europe opens only because two Asian doors close. Reformed missiology sees here the sovereignty of the Spirit over missional geography: the Spirit is not merely the empowerer of human initiative but the director of the mission's course. The church's task is to be obedient to both open doors and closed ones.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Lydia's household was the first European church — gathered in a businesswoman's home around the word of God and the Lord's Supper. Now: The church continues to be built wherever the Lord opens hearts — in homes as often as in purpose-built buildings, through business relationships as often as through formal religious programs.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul came also to Derbe and to Lystra. A disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek. He was well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul came also to Derbe and to Lystra. A disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek. He was well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium.

Meaning first. Acts 16 tells how the gospel crossed into Europe. Paul gains a young helper, Timothy. The Spirit closes doors in Asia and Bithynia, and opens one in a vision: Come over to Macedonia. In Philippi three very different people are saved: Lydia, a wealthy businesswoman whose heart the Lord opened; a slave girl freed from a spirit; and a Roman jailer who asks, What must I do to be saved? Paul and Silas are beaten and jailed, sing at midnight, and see God shake the prison. Every kind of person, every kind of bondage, and one answer: Believe in the Lord Jesus.

A disciple was there, named Timothy. Key words. Timothy’s mother was Eunice and his grandmother Lois, both believers, who taught him the Scriptures from childhood (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15). He became Paul’s closest co-worker, his “true child in the faith” (1 Timothy 1:2), and received two letters. Probably converted during Paul’s first visit, when Paul was stoned (2 Timothy 3:10–11).

The son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek. A mixed marriage. His father, a Gentile, apparently did not believe and had not let his son be circumcised.

He was well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium. A good reputation, a qualification for ministry (1 Timothy 3:7).

In a sentence. Paul came to Derbe and Lystra, where there was a disciple named Timothy, the son of a believing Jewish mother and a Greek father, well spoken of by the believers in Lystra and Iconium.

On a Tuesday. Mothers and grandmothers, teach your children the Scriptures. God may make a Timothy of them.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy’s mother was Eunice and his grandmother Lois. He became Paul’s closest co-worker.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek.

Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him. To replace John Mark as helper.

And he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places. Key words. Surprising, right after the council. But the reason is not salvation; it is mission. Jews regarded the son of a Jewish mother as Jewish. An uncircumcised Jew would be seen as an apostate, and would close synagogue doors to Paul. Paul became a Jew to the Jews to win Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20).

The difference with Titus. Paul would not circumcise Titus when it was demanded as necessary for salvation (Galatians 2:3–5). Titus was a Gentile, and the gospel was at stake. Timothy was ethnically Jewish, and circumcision was a matter of removing an obstacle. The same act can be right or wrong depending on why it is done. When circumcision is demanded as a condition of grace, refuse; when it is chosen to open a door, it can be freedom (1 Corinthians 7:19).

In a sentence. Paul wanted Timothy to go with him, and circumcised him because of the Jews in that area, who all knew his father was a Greek.

For worship. Never compromise the gospel. But be willing to give up your rights to win others.
verseByVerse.note: Paul would not circumcise Titus when it was demanded as necessary for salvation; Timothy, with a Jewish mother, was circumcised to remove an obstacle among Jews.

parallels.desc: to the Jews I became as a Jew

verseByVerse.quote: As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered to them for observance the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem. So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered to them for observance the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem. So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily.

They delivered to them for observance the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders. “Decisions” (dogmata): the council’s decrees. The same Paul who circumcised Timothy delivered the letter that freed Gentiles from circumcision. No contradiction: grace for salvation, love for fellowship.

So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily. Key words. Another progress report (6:7; 9:31). Strength and growth together. Clear teaching about grace strengthens churches.

In a sentence. As they went through the towns, they passed on the decisions of the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, and the churches were strengthened in faith and grew daily in number.

On a Tuesday. Churches grow strong when they understand grace. Teach it clearly.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. And when they had come up to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. And when they had come up to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them.

Having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. Key words. Asia was the Roman province on the west coast of Asia Minor, with Ephesus its capital. Not the continent. Why forbidden? Not that God didn’t care for Asia; Paul would later spend three years in Ephesus (19:10). It was not yet the time. We aren’t told how the Spirit forbade them: a prophecy, an inner conviction, circumstances.

They attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them. Bithynia, in the north. “The Spirit of Jesus”: a unique phrase, showing that the Spirit is the Spirit of the risen Jesus (Romans 8:9; Philippians 1:19). Jesus directs his mission by his Spirit.

Closed doors. Paul and his team didn’t sit and wait. They kept moving, and the Spirit closed doors. God guides moving feet. A closed door is guidance too.

In a sentence. They travelled through Phrygia and Galatia, since the Holy Spirit kept them from speaking the word in Asia, and when they reached Mysia they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus would not let them.

On a Tuesday. When God closes a door, trust him. He is leading you somewhere else.
verseByVerse.note: Asia was the Roman province on the west coast of Asia Minor, with Ephesus its chief city. Mysia and Bithynia lay in the north-west.

parallels.desc: all the residents of Asia heard the word

verseByVerse.quote: "So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas.

So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas. Troas was a port on the Aegean coast, near ancient Troy. They had come as far as they could go. The sea was before them. Perhaps they were puzzled. God had a plan.

In a sentence. So they passed by Mysia and went down to Troas.

For worship. When you reach the end of your road, God has a way you haven’t seen.
verseByVerse.note: Troas was a port on the Aegean coast, near ancient Troy.

verseByVerse.quote: And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him and saying, "Come over to Macedonia and help us." And when Paul had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him and saying, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” And when Paul had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.

A man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him and saying, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” Key words. Macedonia was the Roman province of northern Greece, the gospel’s first entry into Europe. The cry for help: the world’s deepest need, though it doesn’t know it, is the gospel.

Immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia. Key words. “We”: the first of the “we” passages (16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16), where Luke joins the story as an eyewitness. Luke may have joined Paul at Troas, perhaps as his doctor.

Concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them. “Concluding” (symbibazontes): putting it together. The closed doors, the vision, and the team’s discernment together showed God’s will. Guidance is often confirmed by putting the pieces together, with others.

In a sentence. In the night Paul had a vision of a man from Macedonia standing and begging him to come over and help them, and after this vision they immediately set out for Macedonia, concluding that God had called them to preach the gospel there.

For worship. The world is crying, “Come and help us.” Answer with the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Macedonia was the Roman province of northern Greece — the gospel’s first step into Europe. Here “we” appears: Luke, the author, joins the journey.

parallels.desc: further “we” passages

verseByVerse.quote: "So, setting sail from Troas, we made a direct voyage to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. We remained in this city some days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, setting sail from Troas, we made a direct voyage to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. We remained in this city some days.

We made a direct voyage to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis. A quick crossing with a following wind, two days. (The return trip took five, 20:6.) Neapolis was Philippi’s port.

And from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. Key words. Philippi was a Roman colony, settled by veterans, a little Rome abroad, proud of Roman law and citizenship. Named after Philip of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great. Paul later wrote to the church here: our citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20), a phrase they would understand.

In a sentence. Sailing from Troas, they went straight to Samothrace, the next day to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi, a leading city of that part of Macedonia and a Roman colony, where they stayed some days.

On a Tuesday. You are a citizen of heaven living in a colony on earth. Live by its laws.
verseByVerse.note: Neapolis was Philippi’s port. Philippi was a Roman colony, settled with army veterans, governed like a little Rome.

parallels.desc: our citizenship is in heaven

verseByVerse.quote: "And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together.

And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer. There was apparently no synagogue; Jews met to pray in the open by the river. A synagogue needed ten Jewish men; Philippi didn’t have them. The River Gangites, west of the city.

And we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together. Key words. The first gospel preaching in Europe was to a women’s prayer meeting by a river. Paul, the former Pharisee, sat down and taught women. The gospel honours women.

In a sentence. On the Sabbath they went outside the city gate to the river, where they expected to find a place of prayer, and sat down and spoke to the women gathered there.

For worship. Great things can begin in small prayer meetings. Don’t despise them.
verseByVerse.note: There was apparently no synagogue; Jews met to pray in the open, by the river.

verseByVerse.quote: One who heard us was a woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. And after she was baptized, and her household as well, she urged us, saying, "If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay." And she prevailed upon us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One who heard us was a woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. And after she was baptized, and her household as well, she urged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay.” And she prevailed upon us.

A woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods. Thyatira, in Asia, was famous for its purple dye; purple cloth was a luxury for the wealthy. Lydia was a businesswoman, probably well off, with a house large enough to host the team and the church (v. 40). Thyatira was in the province of Asia, where the Spirit had forbidden them to preach; now an Asian is converted in Europe.

Who was a worshiper of God. A God-fearing Gentile.

The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. Key words. One of the clearest statements of God’s work in conversion. Paul spoke; the Lord opened. Paul could reach her ears; only the Lord could open her heart. This is effectual grace: God opens hearts to receive the gospel (2 Corinthians 4:6; Ephesians 1:18). Lydia did pay attention, really, freely; but she did so because the Lord opened her heart. Both human preaching and divine opening are needed.

And after she was baptized, and her household as well. Her household: servants, and perhaps children.

Where Christians differ: household baptisms. Paedobaptists see household baptisms as including infants, and so supporting infant baptism. Verdict: no infants are mentioned in any household baptism in Acts. In the jailer’s case, the word was spoken to all in the house and the whole household believed and rejoiced (vv. 32, 34). In Cornelius’s, all heard and received the Spirit (10:44). The households baptised were households who heard and believed. Credobaptists hold this charitably, respecting brothers and sisters who read it differently.

If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay. Faith shows itself at once in hospitality. The first church in Europe met in her home.

In a sentence. One of the listeners was Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira who worshipped God, and the Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message, and after she and her household were baptised, she urged them to stay at her home if they judged her faithful to the Lord, and persuaded them.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the Lord to open hearts as you speak. You can reach ears; only he can reach hearts.
verseByVerse.note: Thyatira, in Asia, was famous for its purple dye; purple cloth was a luxury. A “worshiper of God” was a Gentile who worshipped Israel’s God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–40 — Prison and Earthquake in Philippi
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A slave girl whose fortune-telling earned money for her owners follows the missionaries for days, shouting that they are servants of the Most High God, until Paul casts the spirit out of her in Jesus’ name. Her owners, robbed of their profit, drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates, accusing them as Jews of promoting un-Roman customs. They are stripped, beaten with rods and fastened in the stocks. At midnight, as they pray and sing hymns, an earthquake opens every door and loosens every chain. The jailer, about to kill himself, is stopped by Paul, falls before them and asks what he must do to be saved. They tell him to believe in the Lord Jesus, and speak the word to his whole household.
