verseByVerse.quote: "And as they were seeking to kill him, word came to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion. He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. And when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as they were seeking to kill him, word came to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion. He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. And when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.

As they were seeking to kill him. A lynching.

Word came to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion. The tribune commanded the cohort of Roman soldiers stationed in the Antonia Fortress, next to the temple, about a thousand men. They watched the temple courts closely at festivals.

He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. “Centurions,” plural: at least two hundred men.

And when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul. Key words. Rescued by pagan soldiers. God used Rome to protect his servant, as he promised (23:11).

In a sentence. As they were trying to kill him, news reached the commander of the Roman troops that all Jerusalem was in uproar, and he immediately took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them, and when the crowd saw them, they stopped beating Paul.

For worship. God’s protection can come from unexpected places. Thank him for governments that restrain violence.
verseByVerse.note: The tribune commanded the cohort of Roman soldiers stationed in the Antonia Fortress, which overlooked the temple courts.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the tribune came up and arrested him and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He inquired who he was and what he had done."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the tribune came up and arrested him and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He inquired who he was and what he had done.

Then the tribune came up and arrested him and ordered him to be bound with two chains. Key words. Agabus’s prophecy fulfilled (v. 11). Bound, perhaps between two soldiers. From now to the end of Acts, Paul is a prisoner.

He inquired who he was and what he had done. He assumed the victim was the criminal.

In a sentence. The commander came up, arrested him, ordered him bound with two chains, and asked who he was and what he had done.

On a Tuesday. Paul’s chains were part of God’s plan. Your hardships may be too.

verseByVerse.quote: "Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, some another. And as he could not learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered him to be brought into the barracks. And when he came to the steps, he was actually carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, some another. And as he could not learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered him to be brought into the barracks. And when he came to the steps, he was actually carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd,

Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, some another. As in Ephesus (19:32). Mobs don’t think.

He ordered him to be brought into the barracks. The Antonia Fortress.

And when he came to the steps. Steps led from the temple courts up into the fortress. Josephus describes them.

He was actually carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd. Lifted up off his feet to get him away.

In a sentence. Some in the crowd shouted one thing and some another, and since the commander couldn’t learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered Paul taken into the barracks, and when they reached the steps the soldiers had to carry him because of the violence of the mob.

For worship. When the crowd rages, God carries his servants through.
verseByVerse.note: Steps led from the temple courts up into the fortress.

verseByVerse.quote: "for the mob of the people followed, crying out, 'Away with him!'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
for the mob of the people followed, crying out, “Away with him!”

For the mob of the people followed, crying out, “Away with him!” Key words. The same cry as against Jesus (Luke 23:18; John 19:15). Paul shares his Lord’s rejection, in the same city, perhaps on the same spot where Jesus was condemned.

In a sentence. The crowd followed, shouting, “Away with him!”

On a Tuesday. To share Christ’s rejection is to share his honour. Don’t be ashamed of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the tribune, 'May I say something to you?' And he said, 'Do you know Greek? Are you not the Egyptian, then, who recently stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the tribune, “May I say something to you?” And he said, “Do you know Greek? Are you not the Egyptian, then, who recently stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?”

May I say something to you? In polished Greek, after a beating. Remarkable composure.

Do you know Greek? Surprised. An educated man.

Are you not the Egyptian, then, who recently stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness? Key words. The historian Josephus describes an Egyptian false prophet who led a crowd to the Mount of Olives, promising Jerusalem’s walls would fall at his command. The Roman governor Felix attacked; many were killed, but the Egyptian escaped. The “Assassins” (sikarioi, dagger-men) were Jewish terrorists who stabbed opponents in crowds. Luke’s history matches Josephus.

In a sentence. As he was about to be taken into the barracks, Paul asked the commander if he might say something, and the commander asked if he spoke Greek, and whether he wasn’t the Egyptian who had recently led a revolt and taken four thousand terrorists into the desert.

For worship. God’s servants are often mistaken for troublemakers. Let your life show who you really are.
verseByVerse.note: The historian Josephus describes an Egyptian false prophet who led followers to the Mount of Olives a few years earlier and escaped when the Romans attacked. The “Assassins” were extremists who stabbed opponents with hidden daggers in crowds.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul replied, 'I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city. I beg you, permit me to speak to the people.' And when he had given him permission, Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people. And when there was a great hush, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul replied, “I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city. I beg you, permit me to speak to the people.” And when he had given him permission, Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people. And when there was a great hush, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying:

I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city. Tarsus was a proud and prosperous city, known for learning, with a famous university. Paul was a citizen of Tarsus, and of Rome (22:25).

I beg you, permit me to speak to the people. Key words. Beaten, chained, nearly killed, and his first wish is to preach to those who attacked him. A heart for his people (Romans 9:1–3).

Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people. A dramatic scene: the prisoner, in chains, on the steps, facing the mob.

And when there was a great hush, he addressed them in the Hebrew language. Probably Aramaic, the language of Jews in the land. Hearing their own tongue, they fell silent (22:2).

In a sentence. Paul answered that he was a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of an important city, and asked permission to speak to the people, and when it was given, he stood on the steps and motioned to the crowd, and when they were silent, he spoke to them in Hebrew.

On a Tuesday. Love those who hate you, and look for every chance to tell them of Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Tarsus was a proud and prosperous city, known for learning. The “Hebrew language” was probably Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in Judea.

21.theology: The Will of God and the Path of Suffering. Acts 21 presents with unusual clarity the Reformed conviction that the will of God is not always comfortable, and that knowing it does not mean avoiding what it contains. Paul knows chains await. He goes anyway. His companions know Paul knows. They submit anyway. “Let the will of the Lord be done” is not fatalism — it is the active, willing submission of people who have learned that God’s purposes are worked out through suffering, not around it. This is the theology of Romans 8:28 embodied in a house in Caesarea: all things — including imprisonment, beatings, and the howling of a mob — work together for good for those who love God and are called according to his purpose. Paul’s chains will take him to Rome. God knew this. Paul submitted to it. Rome receives the gospel.
21.examples:
Then: A man walking knowingly toward chains, accompanied by weeping friends who have said everything they can say and now can only pray. A church in Jerusalem that receives the Gentile mission report with joy and then watches its guest arrested in the temple court. The will of the Lord, being done — at great cost, with great grief, toward a great purpose that none of them can yet see fully.

Now: The church in every age must learn the grammar of “let the will of the Lord be done.” It is learned most deeply in the moments when the will of the Lord leads into what we would not choose — illness, loss, rejection, persecution. Paul goes to Jerusalem not because it is easy or because he can see the outcome, but because the Spirit has said go and the Lord has said trust. This is the faith that follows a Lord who himself prayed “not my will, but yours.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul addresses the crowd as brothers and fathers, and when they hear him speak in their own tongue they grow quieter. He tells them he is a Jew born in Tarsus, raised in Jerusalem and trained precisely in the ancestral law under Gamaliel, as zealous for God as they are. He hunted the Way to the death, arresting men and women, with the authority of the high priest and the council. On the road to Damascus at midday a blinding light flashed round him; he fell and heard a voice asking why he was persecuting him. He asked who was speaking, and the voice answered that it was Jesus of Nazareth. His companions saw the light but did not grasp the voice. Told to go into Damascus to learn what he must do, he was led there blind. Ananias, a devout and respected keeper of the law, came and restored his sight, and told him the God of their fathers had chosen him to know his will, see the Righteous One and be his witness to all people. He urged him to be baptised and have his sins washed away, calling on his name. Later, praying in the temple in Jerusalem, Paul fell into a trance and saw the Lord, who told him to leave quickly because they would not accept his testimony. Paul protested that they knew how he had persecuted believers and had approved Stephen’s death. But the Lord replied that he was sending him far away to the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sovereign Grace, and a Commission Older Than the Convert

Ananias's word for what God did to Saul is appointed — chosen and designated (22:14) — and Paul never forgot it, writing later that God had set me apart before I was born (Gal. 1:15). The light at noon was not God changing his mind about Saul of Tarsus. It was God keeping an appointment made before Saul existed. Nothing in the account belongs to the convert: Christ sought him, struck him down, named him in his mother tongue, blinded him, and told him what he would do. Paul did not find Jesus; Jesus took Paul.

Two guards keep this from being abstract. First, on the timing of the new birth Scripture is deliberately reticent, and we should be too — regeneration is the Spirit's secret work, known by its fruits and not by a stopwatch (see the note at vv. 9–10). Second, on wash away your sins (v. 16), the sign is spoken of in the language of the thing signified, as Scripture habitually does; the blood of Christ does the washing and baptism seals and publishes it, which is exactly how Paul afterwards handled circumcision as a seal of a righteousness already had by faith (Rom. 4:11).

And the chapter's summit is what grace does with a specific, named, unforgettable sin. The man who guarded the garments at Stephen's stoning is sent to the ends of the earth with Stephen's message. That is not grace overlooking a small thing. It is the blood of the Righteous One proving stronger than the blood that was shed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A frightened disciple in Damascus was given the address of the man holding warrants for his arrest, and went. He knew his own name was probably on the list. He knocked, walked into the one house in the city where a Christian could be seized on the spot, and said two words before anything had been proved about the blind man sitting there: Brother Saul.

Now: Picture the person whose arrival in your church on Sunday would be hardest to absorb — not a stranger, but someone with a history, and a history with you. Somebody who did real damage and knew what they were doing. Now suppose the Lord has laid hold of them. How long, in practice, before anyone says brother, and means it, and stops watching the door? Ananias managed it in three days, before any evidence of change had been produced, because he understood that the church does not decide who its family is. It recognises whom the Lord has already taken in.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Brothers and fathers, hear the defense that I now make before you.' And when they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even more quiet. And he said:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers and fathers, hear the defense that I now make before you. And when they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even more quiet. And he said:

Meaning first. Acts 22 is Paul’s defence to the Jerusalem crowd from the steps of the fortress. Paul’s first defence, to the Jerusalem crowd. He tells his own story: a zealous Jew, trained by Gamaliel, a persecutor of the Way, until Jesus met him on the Damascus road. He stresses everything that would connect with his hearers. They listen, until he says the word “Gentiles.” Then the riot erupts again. Paul is about to be flogged, and claims his Roman citizenship. Personal testimony, honestly told, is one of the gospel’s great tools; and it shows that Paul’s mission to the Gentiles came from Christ himself.

Brothers and fathers, hear the defense that I now make before you. Key words. “Brothers and fathers”: as Stephen began (7:2). Respectful, even to the mob that just beat him. “Defense” (apologias): the word that gives us apologetics, a reasoned defence (1 Peter 3:15).

When they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even more quiet. Their heart language. He is one of them.

In a sentence. Paul asked his brothers and fathers to hear his defence, and when they heard him speaking in Hebrew, they became even quieter.

On a Tuesday. Speak to people in a way they can understand, with respect, even when they oppose you.
verseByVerse.note: Paul’s first defence, to the Jerusalem crowd.

parallels.desc: Stephen’s same opening

verseByVerse.quote: "'I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strict manner of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God as all of you are this day. I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering to prison both men and women,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strict manner of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God as all of you are this day. I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering to prison both men and women,

I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city. Born abroad, raised in Jerusalem from youth (26:4).

Educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strict manner of the law of our fathers. Key words. Gamaliel was the most respected Pharisee teacher of the day (5:34); students sat at the teacher’s feet. Paul had the best Jewish education available. He was a Pharisee of Pharisees (Philippians 3:5–6; Galatians 1:14).

Being zealous for God as all of you are this day. Key words. A gracious point of contact: he understands their zeal, because he had it. He doesn’t mock them; he says, I was like you. Zeal without knowledge (Romans 10:2).

I persecuted this Way to the death. Honest about his past.

In a sentence. Paul said he was a Jew, born in Tarsus but raised in Jerusalem, trained by Gamaliel in the strict law of their fathers, as zealous for God as they were, and had persecuted the Way to the death, arresting and imprisoning men and women.

For worship. Zeal is good, but zeal without knowledge of Christ can do terrible harm. Pray for the zealous who don’t know him.
verseByVerse.note: Gamaliel was the most respected Pharisee teacher of the day; students sat at their teacher’s feet.

verseByVerse.quote: "'as the high priest and the whole council of elders can bear me witness. From them I received letters to the brothers, and I journeyed toward Damascus to take those also who were there and bring them in bonds to Jerusalem to be punished. As I was on my way and drew near to Damascus, about noon a great light from heaven suddenly shone around me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
as the high priest and the whole council of elders can bear me witness. From them I received letters to the brothers, and I journeyed toward Damascus to take those also who were there and bring them in bonds to Jerusalem to be punished. As I was on my way and drew near to Damascus, about noon a great light from heaven suddenly shone around me.

As the high priest and the whole council of elders can bear me witness. Check the records. Verifiable facts.

From them I received letters to the brothers. “The brothers”: the Jews of Damascus. Paul still calls them brothers.

About noon a great light from heaven suddenly shone around me. Key words. Noon: the brightest time of day, and the light outshone the sun (26:13). A new detail, unmistakable.

In a sentence. The high priest and council could confirm it, since he got letters from them to the Jews in Damascus and went to bring the believers there back to Jerusalem in chains for punishment, but as he neared Damascus around noon, a great light from heaven suddenly blazed around him.

On a Tuesday. Christianity rests on facts that can be checked. Your faith is not a fairy tale.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" And I answered, "Who are you, Lord?" And he said to me, "I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’ And I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And he said to me, ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.’

Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? As in 9:4.

I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting. Key words. “Of Nazareth”: added here, for the Jerusalem crowd. The despised man from Nazareth, whom they had crucified, is the Lord of glory speaking from heaven.

In a sentence. He fell to the ground and heard a voice asking why he was persecuting him, and when he asked who it was, the voice said, “I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.”

For worship. Jesus of Nazareth reigns from heaven. Bow to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Now those who were with me saw the light but did not understand the voice of the one who was speaking to me. And I said, "What shall I do, Lord?" And the Lord said to me, "Rise, and go into Damascus, and there you will be told all that is appointed for you to do."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now those who were with me saw the light but did not understand the voice of the one who was speaking to me. And I said, ‘What shall I do, Lord?’ And the Lord said to me, ‘Rise, and go into Damascus, and there you will be told all that is appointed for you to do.’

Now those who were with me saw the light but did not understand the voice of the one who was speaking to me. Key words. His companions saw the light and heard a sound but could not understand the words (9:7 says they heard the voice; here, they didn’t understand it). The Greek verb “hear” (akouō) can mean hear a sound or understand speech. No contradiction: they heard, but did not understand.

What shall I do, Lord? Key words. The question of a new disciple. Total surrender. “Lord”: he has a new master.

There you will be told all that is appointed for you to do. “Appointed”: his task was already set by God.

In a sentence. His companions saw the light but did not understand the voice speaking to him, and he asked what he should do, and the Lord told him to get up and go into Damascus, where he would be told all that had been appointed for him.

On a Tuesday. Ask each day: What shall I do, Lord?
verseByVerse.note: His companions saw the light and heard a sound but could not make out the words.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And since I could not see because of the brightness of that light, I was led by the hand by those who were with me, and came into Damascus. And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And since I could not see because of the brightness of that light, I was led by the hand by those who were with me, and came into Damascus. And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there,

I could not see because of the brightness of that light. Blinded by glory.

And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there. Key words. To the Jerusalem crowd, Paul stresses Ananias’s Jewish piety, not his Christian discipleship (9:10). A law-keeping Jew, respected by Jews, brought God’s message to him. Wise testimony: emphasise what connects with your hearers.

In a sentence. Blinded by the brilliance of the light, he was led by the hand into Damascus, where a man named Ananias, devout in keeping the law and highly respected by all the Jews there...

For worship. Be thoughtful in how you tell your story. Emphasise what helps your hearers.

verseByVerse.quote: "'came to me, and standing by me said to me, "Brother Saul, receive your sight." And at that very hour I received my sight and saw him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
came to me, and standing by me said to me, ‘Brother Saul, receive your sight.’ And at that very hour I received my sight and saw him.

Brother Saul, receive your sight. The tender greeting (9:17).

And at that very hour I received my sight and saw him. Instant.

In a sentence. Ananias stood beside him and said, “Brother Saul, receive your sight,” and at that moment he could see him.

On a Tuesday. A kind word can open blind eyes. Speak one today.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And he said, "The God of our fathers appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth; for you will be a witness for him to everyone of what you have seen and heard."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said, ‘The God of our fathers appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth; for you will be a witness for him to everyone of what you have seen and heard.

The God of our fathers appointed you. Key words. Not a new God, but Israel’s God. “Appointed” (proecheirisato): chose beforehand, selected. Sovereign choice.

To know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth. “The Righteous One” is a title for the Messiah (3:14; 7:52). Paul saw the risen Christ, the basis of his apostleship (1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:8).

For you will be a witness for him to everyone of what you have seen and heard. “Everyone”: not just Jews. Paul is preparing for the word that will set them off.

In a sentence. Ananias said the God of their fathers had chosen him to know his will, see the Righteous One and hear him speak, for he would be his witness to everyone of what he had seen and heard.

For worship. You too are a witness to everyone of what you have seen and heard of Christ.
verseByVerse.note: “The Righteous One” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now why do you wait? Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name.' When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now why do you wait? Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name.’ When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance

And now why do you wait? Urgency.

Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name. Key words. In Greek: having risen, be baptised, and wash away your sins, calling on his name. The washing of sins is linked with calling on his name. It is faith, calling on Christ, that receives forgiveness (2:21; Romans 10:13); baptism is its outward sign and seal.

Where Christians differ: does baptism wash away sins? Some take this verse to teach that the water of baptism itself removes sin. Verdict: Saul had already met the risen Lord, called him Lord, and been addressed as “brother” before his baptism. Sins are washed away by the blood of Christ (1 John 1:7; Revelation 1:5), received by faith; baptism is the God-given picture and seal of that washing (1 Peter 3:21: not the removal of dirt from the body, but the appeal to God for a good conscience). Baptism should not be delayed, but it is not the cause of forgiveness.

When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple. Key words. Paul stresses that he prayed in the temple. He had not abandoned it; he honoured it.

I fell into a trance. A vision.

In a sentence. Ananias asked what he was waiting for, and told him to get up, be baptised and wash his sins away, calling on the Lord’s name; and when Paul returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, he fell into a trance.

On a Tuesday. If you believe and haven’t been baptised, why wait?

verseByVerse.quote: "'and saw him saying to me, "Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me." And I said, "Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
and saw him saying to me, ‘Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me.’ And I said, ‘Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you.

Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me. Key words. Jesus himself told Paul to leave Jerusalem. A new detail (compare 9:29–30). Jerusalem would reject him.

Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you. Paul argued with the Lord: surely they will listen to me, since they know what I was. A natural hope. He thought his conversion would convince them.

In a sentence. In the vision, the Lord told him to leave Jerusalem quickly, because they would not accept his testimony, and Paul answered that they knew he had gone from synagogue to synagogue imprisoning and beating believers.

For worship. Our hopes for how God will use us are not always his plans. Trust his wisdom.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing by and approving and watching over the garments of those who killed him.' And he said to me, "Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing by and approving and watching over the garments of those who killed him.’ And he said to me, ‘Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’

And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed. Key words. “Witness” (martyros): the word that came to mean martyr, one who dies for his testimony. Stephen was the first.

I myself was standing by and approving and watching over the garments of those who killed him. Paul never forgot it (1 Corinthians 15:9; 1 Timothy 1:13). Grace doesn’t erase memory, but it removes guilt.

Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles. Key words. The word that would set off the crowd. Jesus sent Paul to the Gentiles. Paul’s mission was not his own idea, but Christ’s command, given in the temple.

In a sentence. Paul told the Lord that when the blood of his witness Stephen was shed, he stood by approving and guarding the clothes of those who killed him, but the Lord said, “Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.”

For worship. God turns persecutors into preachers. No past is too dark for his grace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–30 — The Roman Custody and Paul's Citizenship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the word “Gentiles” the crowd erupts, shouting that such a man should be wiped off the earth, tearing off their cloaks and throwing dust into the air. The commander orders Paul into the barracks to be flogged and questioned, to discover why they are shouting against him. As they stretch him out for the lash, Paul asks the centurion whether it is lawful to flog a Roman citizen who has not been condemned. The centurion warns the commander, who comes and asks Paul directly whether he is a citizen. Paul says yes. The commander says that his own citizenship cost him a great deal; Paul answers that he was born a citizen. Those about to interrogate him withdraw at once, and the commander is alarmed at having put a citizen in chains. Next day, wanting to know exactly what the Jews accuse him of, he releases Paul and orders the chief priests and the whole council to assemble, and brings Paul before them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Rights as Tools, Not Shields

Paul's Roman citizenship is one of the clearest case studies in Scripture of how a Christian may handle a legitimate privilege. He does not renounce it, and he does not hide behind it. At Philippi he took the beating with the card in his pocket and produced it only the next morning (16:37), because that beating served the gospel and produced a jailer's household. On the barracks steps one chapter ago he deliberately withheld it, because he wanted a pulpit and not a rescue (21:39). Here he plays it, seconds before the whip falls, because a scourging would have ended a man who has been told he must testify at Rome.

The deciding question is never what will hurt least. It is what will serve most. That is a harder rule than either renouncing rights or clinging to them, because it has to be asked fresh every time and it cannot be settled in advance by policy.

Underneath it lies the Reformed conviction about the civil magistrate. God gave the sword to the state (Rom. 13:4), and he uses it — often through officials with no interest in him at all. A centurion protecting his own career, a commander doing the arithmetic on his pension, an empire enforcing its own statutes: none of them knows he is keeping the apostle to the Gentiles alive and moving him toward Rome. God's providence does not require the cooperation of the people it employs.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Four officials in turn — Lysias, Felix, Festus and Agrippa — examined the case against Paul, and not one of them could name a crime. The tribune could not learn the facts in the uproar, and wrote that he found nothing deserving death or imprisonment (23:29). Festus said the accusers brought no charge of the sort he had expected (25:18) and finally admitted it was unreasonable to send on a prisoner without indicating the charges (25:27). Luke records all four without a word of editorial.

Now: Where the church is opposed, it is worth being clear about which thing is happening. Sometimes Christians are disciplined for genuine wrongdoing, and the right response is repentance, not a persecution narrative. But when the file keeps coming back empty — when the offence turns out to be the message itself, and no one can state a charge — that is the pattern of this chapter, and the answer is not outrage. It is to keep doing exactly what the empty file says you were doing, and to go on asking, as Paul did with his back to a whipping post, for permission to speak.

verseByVerse.quote: "Up to this word they listened to him. Then they raised their voices and said, 'Away with such a fellow from the earth! For he should not be allowed to live.' And as they were shouting and throwing off their cloaks and flinging dust into the air,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Up to this word they listened to him. Then they raised their voices and said, “Away with such a fellow from the earth! For he should not be allowed to live.” And as they were shouting and throwing off their cloaks and flinging dust into the air,

Up to this word they listened to him. Key words. “This word”: Gentiles. They could accept a vision, even a converted persecutor, but not that God would send a Jew to save Gentiles without making them Jews. National pride was their stumbling block. As at Nazareth, when Jesus mentioned God’s grace to Gentiles (Luke 4:25–29).

Away with such a fellow from the earth! For he should not be allowed to live. “Away with him” again (21:36).

Throwing off their cloaks and flinging dust into the air. Throwing dust in the air and tearing off cloaks were gestures of rage and horror, as at blasphemy, or as preparation for stoning (7:58).

In a sentence. The crowd listened until he said this, then shouted, “Rid the earth of him! He isn’t fit to live!”, throwing off their cloaks and flinging dust into the air.

On a Tuesday. Pride in our group can blind us to God’s grace for others. Watch for it.
verseByVerse.note: Throwing dust in the air and tearing off cloaks were gestures of outrage.

verseByVerse.quote: "the tribune ordered him to be brought into the barracks, saying that he should be examined by flogging, to find out why they were shouting against him like this. But when they had stretched him out for the whips, Paul said to the centurion who was standing by, 'Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and uncondemned?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
the tribune ordered him to be brought into the barracks, saying that he should be examined by flogging, to find out why they were shouting against him like this. But when they had stretched him out for the whips, Paul said to the centurion who was standing by, “Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and uncondemned?”

The tribune ordered him to be brought into the barracks, saying that he should be examined by flogging. Key words. Roman interrogation of non-citizens often used the scourge; citizens were exempt. The scourge (flagellum) was a whip with bone or metal pieces; it could cripple or kill. Jesus was scourged (John 19:1). The tribune didn’t understand Aramaic, so he wanted the truth by torture.

But when they had stretched him out for the whips. Tied, bent over a post, ready.

Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and uncondemned? Key words. A calm question at the last moment. Two crimes: flogging a citizen, and without trial. Christians may use legal rights to protect themselves and the gospel (16:37).

In a sentence. The commander ordered Paul taken into the barracks and interrogated under the whip to find out why they were shouting against him, but as they stretched him out for the lashes, Paul asked the centurion standing there whether it was legal to flog a Roman citizen who had not been found guilty.

For worship. There is a time to suffer silently and a time to claim your rights. Ask God for wisdom to know which.
verseByVerse.note: Roman interrogation of non-citizens often used the scourge; flogging an uncondemned Roman citizen was illegal.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the centurion heard this, he went to the tribune and said to him, 'What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman citizen.' So the tribune came and said to him, 'Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?' And he said, 'Yes.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the centurion heard this, he went to the tribune and said to him, “What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman citizen.” So the tribune came and said to him, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” And he said, “Yes.”

What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman citizen. The centurion knew the law. To flog a citizen could cost the tribune his career.

Tell me, are you a Roman citizen? Falsely claiming citizenship was punishable by death, so the claim was usually believed.

And he said, “Yes.” A one-word answer.

In a sentence. When the centurion heard this, he went and told the commander that this man was a Roman citizen, so the commander came and asked Paul if he was a citizen, and he said yes.

On a Tuesday. God had prepared Paul’s protection before he was born, by his citizenship. His providence reaches far ahead.

verseByVerse.quote: "The tribune answered, 'I bought this citizenship for a large sum.' Paul said, 'But I am a citizen by birth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tribune answered, “I bought this citizenship for a large sum.” Paul said, “But I am a citizen by birth.”

I bought this citizenship for a large sum. Citizenship could be bought through bribes under Claudius. The historian Dio Cassius says it became cheap under Claudius, with officials selling it. The tribune’s name was Claudius Lysias (23:26): he took the emperor’s name with his citizenship.

But I am a citizen by birth. Key words. Paul was born a citizen, higher in status than the tribune. His father or grandfather had received it, perhaps for service to Rome. God’s providence prepared it long before. And Paul tells of another citizenship, given freely, in heaven (Philippians 3:20).

In a sentence. The commander said he had bought his citizenship for a lot of money, and Paul said he was born a citizen.

For worship. Your heavenly citizenship was not bought by you, but for you, with Christ’s blood.
verseByVerse.note: Citizenship could be bought through bribes under Claudius. Paul was born a citizen, probably because his father or grandfather had been granted it.

verseByVerse.quote: "So those who were about to examine him withdrew from him immediately, and the tribune also was afraid, for he realized that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had bound him. But on the next day, desiring to know the real reason why he was being accused by the Jews, he unbound him and commanded the chief priests and all the council to meet, and he brought Paul down and set him before them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So those who were about to examine him withdrew from him immediately, and the tribune also was afraid, for he realized that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had bound him. But on the next day, desiring to know the real reason why he was being accused by the Jews, he unbound him and commanded the chief priests and all the council to meet, and he brought Paul down and set him before them.

Those who were about to examine him withdrew from him immediately. Fear of the consequences.

And the tribune also was afraid, for he realized that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had bound him. Even chaining a citizen without trial was illegal.

Desiring to know the real reason why he was being accused by the Jews. A Roman wanting justice. He couldn’t get it from the mob.

He unbound him and commanded the chief priests and all the council to meet. The council is the Sanhedrin, the same council that condemned Jesus and Stephen. Now Paul stands before it.

In a sentence. Those about to interrogate him backed away at once, and the commander was alarmed to realise he had put a Roman citizen in chains, and the next day, wanting to learn the real charges, he released him, ordered the chief priests and the whole council to meet, and brought Paul to stand before them.

On a Tuesday. God was moving Paul step by step towards Rome, through courts and councils. He orders your steps too.
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin.

22.title: Paul's Defence Before the Crowd
22.text: <sup>1</sup>“Brothers and fathers, hear the defense that I now make before you.” <sup>2</sup>And when they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even more quiet. And he said: <sup>3</sup>“I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strict manner of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God as all of you are this day. <sup>4</sup>I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering to prison both men and women, <sup>5</sup>as the high priest and the whole council of elders can bear me witness. From them I received letters to the brothers, and I journeyed toward Damascus to take those also who were there and bring them in bonds to Jerusalem to be punished. <sup>6</sup>“As I was on my way and drew near to Damascus, about noon a great light from heaven suddenly shone around me. <sup>7</sup>And I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’ <sup>8</sup>And I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And he said to me, ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.’ <sup>9</sup>Now those who were with me saw the light but did not understand the voice of the one who was speaking to me. <sup>10</sup>And I said, ‘What shall I do, Lord?’ And the Lord said to me, ‘Rise, and go into Damascus, and there you will be told all that is appointed for you to do.’ <sup>11</sup>And since I could not see because of the brightness of that light, I was led by the hand by those who were with me, and came into Damascus. <sup>12</sup>“And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there, <sup>13</sup>came to me, and standing by me said to me, ‘Brother Saul, receive your sight.’ And at that very hour I received my sight and saw him. <sup>14</sup>And he said, ‘The God of our fathers appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth; <sup>15</sup>for you will be a witness for him to everyone of what you have seen and heard. <sup>16</sup>And now why do you wait? Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name.’ <sup>17</sup>“When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance <sup>18</sup>and saw him saying to me, ‘Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me.’ <sup>19</sup>And I said, ‘Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you. <sup>20</sup>And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing by and approving and watching over the garments of those who killed him.’ <sup>21</sup>And he said to me, ‘Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’” <sup>22</sup>Up to this word they listened to him. Then they raised their voices and said, “Away with such a fellow from the earth! For he should not be allowed to live.” <sup>23</sup>And as they were shouting and throwing off their cloaks and flinging dust into the air, <sup>24</sup>the tribune ordered him to be brought into the barracks, saying that he should be examined by flogging, to find out why they were shouting against him like this. <sup>25</sup>But when they had stretched him out for the whips, Paul said to the centurion who was standing by, “Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and uncondemned?” <sup>26</sup>When the centurion heard this, he went to the tribune and said to him, “What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman citizen.” <sup>27</sup>So the tribune came and said to him, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” And he said, “Yes.” <sup>28</sup>The tribune answered, “I bought this citizenship for a large sum.” Paul said, “But I am a citizen by birth.” <sup>29</sup>So those who were about to examine him withdrew from him immediately, and the tribune also was afraid, for he realized that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had bound him. <sup>30</sup>But on the next day, desiring to know the real reason why he was being accused by the Jews, he unbound him and commanded the chief priests and all the council to meet, and he brought Paul down and set him before them.
22.overview:
From the steps of the Antonia Fortress Paul speaks to the crowd that has just tried to kill him. This is the second of three accounts of his conversion in Acts (9:1–19; 26:9–18), each shaped for its audience. Here, before a Jewish crowd and in their own language, he stresses how Jewish he is: trained under Gamaliel, zealous for the law, a persecutor of the Way; Ananias is a devout law-keeper; the God who called him is “the God of our fathers”; and his commission came in a vision in the temple itself.

The crowd listens until he says that the Lord sent him to the Gentiles. Then they explode. The tribune orders him to be examined under the lash, but as they stretch him out Paul asks whether it is legal to flog an uncondemned Roman citizen. The tribune, who bought his own citizenship, learns that Paul was born a citizen, and is alarmed. To find out the real charge, he summons the Sanhedrin the next day. Luke shows again that the real offence of Paul’s gospel is grace to the Gentiles, and that Roman law protects the messenger.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Before the Sanhedrin and the Plot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul looks steadily at the council and says he has lived before God with a wholly clear conscience. The high priest Ananias orders those near him to hit him on the mouth. Paul retorts that God will strike him, the whitewashed wall: he sits to judge by the law, yet breaks the law by ordering him struck. When bystanders protest that he is insulting God’s high priest, Paul says he did not realise it was the high priest, for Scripture forbids speaking evil of a ruler of the people. Knowing that the council includes Sadducees and Pharisees, Paul calls out that he is a Pharisee, son of Pharisees, on trial over the hope of the resurrection. This splits the assembly, since Sadducees deny resurrection, angels and spirits, while Pharisees accept them. In the uproar some Pharisee scribes declare him innocent: perhaps a spirit or angel has spoken to him. The dispute turns so violent that the commander, fearing Paul will be torn apart, has soldiers snatch him back into the barracks. The following night the Lord stands beside Paul and tells him to take heart: as he has testified in Jerusalem, so he must testify in Rome. In the morning over forty men vow not to eat or drink until they have killed Paul. They ask the chief priests to request another hearing so they can ambush him on the way. Paul’s nephew hears of the plot and tells Paul, who has a centurion take the young man to the commander. Taken aside, the nephew explains the plan, and the commander sends him away with orders to tell no one.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Promise That Does Not Remove the Danger

Acts 23:11 is the hinge of the second half of the book, and what makes it pastorally useful is as much what it withholds as what it gives. The Lord does not tell Paul he will be released, or comfortable, or vindicated. He does not mention the two years in Caesarea, the storm, or the shipwreck — all of which are still coming, and none of which is cancelled. He gives an assignment and guarantees its completion: you must testify also in Rome. The word is dei, Luke's word for divine necessity, the same word he uses for the sufferings of the Son of Man. Paul's arrival in Rome is now as fixed as the cross.

That is the Reformed doctrine of providence at work, and this chapter shows both halves of it. God ordains the end, and he ordains the means — and the means are startlingly ordinary: a boy who overhears something, an officer protecting his career, a duty roster. Paul believes the promise absolutely and immediately calls a centurion, exactly as he will later believe an angel's word that all aboard will live and then warn that unless the sailors stayed in the ship no one could be saved (27:31). Certainty about the outcome does not make action unnecessary; it makes action possible without panic.

And the instruments need not be godly, or even willing. Claudius Lysias is a self-serving man who falsifies his own report. The Lord uses him unimproved, and he goes off shift with no idea what he has just done.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A conspiracy of more than forty men, sworn under a self-curse, endorsed by the chief priests and elders, with the machinery of the Sanhedrin ready to supply the pretext — defeated by an unnamed young man who happened to hear something and had the nerve to walk across a city and say it out loud. He is never named, never mentioned again, and there is no tradition about him at all. Every consequence of Paul's Roman years runs through his afternoon.

Now: Very few Christians are given a Paul-sized life, and almost every Christian is at some point given the nephew's. You know something. You noticed something. You are standing near enough to do something, and you have about a minute to decide whether it is really your business. The thing that makes this hard is not courage in the heroic sense; it is that the action looks far too small to matter and you will almost certainly never be told how it turned out. He was ordered to keep quiet and sent home. Do it anyway. The size of the outcome has never been the measure of the obedience, and it is not usually visible from where you are standing.

verseByVerse.quote: "And looking intently at the council, Paul said, 'Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day.' And the high priest Ananias commanded those who stood by him to strike him on the mouth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And looking intently at the council, Paul said, “Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day.” And the high priest Ananias commanded those who stood by him to strike him on the mouth.

Meaning first. Acts 23 shows Paul before the Sanhedrin, the council that condemned Jesus. The trial collapses into a quarrel between Pharisees and Sadducees over the resurrection. That night the risen Lord stands by Paul and promises he will testify in Rome. Next morning, forty men vow to kill him; his nephew overhears; and the Roman tribune sends him under a guard of 470 soldiers to the governor at Caesarea. The chapter shows God’s promise kept through ordinary means: a boy’s ears, a soldier’s caution, a Roman letter.

Looking intently at the council. Steady, unafraid.

Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day. Key words. “Lived my life” (pepoliteumai): conducted myself as a citizen, lived as a member of God’s people. A clear conscience before God (24:16; 2 Timothy 1:3). Not sinless, since he persecuted the church, but sincere then, and forgiven now. He addresses them as equals: “brothers,” not “rulers.”

And the high priest Ananias commanded those who stood by him to strike him on the mouth. Ananias was high priest from about AD 47 to 58; Josephus describes him as greedy and violent, seizing the tithes of ordinary priests so that some starved. He was later assassinated by Jewish rebels. Striking an accused man before trial was illegal, as with Jesus (John 18:22).

In a sentence. Paul looked straight at the council and said he had lived before God with a perfectly clear conscience to this day, and the high priest Ananias ordered those near him to strike him on the mouth.

On a Tuesday. Live so that you can say: I have a good conscience before God.
verseByVerse.note: Ananias was high priest from about AD 47 to 58; Josephus describes him as greedy and violent.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then Paul said to him, 'God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! Are you sitting to judge me according to the law, and yet contrary to the law you order me to be struck?' Those who stood by said, 'Would you revile God's high priest?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Paul said to him, “God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! Are you sitting to judge me according to the law, and yet contrary to the law you order me to be struck?” Those who stood by said, “Would you revile God’s high priest?”

God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! Key words. A whitewashed wall looks solid but hides the crumbling beneath (Ezekiel 13:10–15). Jesus called the Pharisees whitewashed tombs (Matthew 23:27). Hypocrisy: outwardly righteous, inwardly corrupt. And God did strike him: he was murdered about ten years later.

Are you sitting to judge me according to the law, and yet contrary to the law you order me to be struck? The law forbade punishing without trial (Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 25:1–2). The judge was breaking the law he was meant to uphold.

Would you revile God’s high priest? Insulting the high priest was serious.

Where Christians differ: was Paul wrong to speak this way? Some contrast Paul’s words with Jesus, who did not revile when reviled (1 Peter 2:23). Verdict: Paul’s words were true and prophetic, and his protest against injustice was right. Yet he immediately acknowledged that speaking evil of a ruler was forbidden (v. 5), showing a humble, teachable spirit. Even apostles could speak in heat. What marks Paul is not perfection, but his quick submission to Scripture when reminded.

In a sentence. Paul said God would strike him, the whitewashed wall, for sitting to judge by the law while breaking it by ordering him struck, and those standing by asked if he dared to insult God’s high priest.

For worship. Hypocrisy is a whitewashed wall. Ask God to make you the same inside as out.
verseByVerse.note: A whitewashed wall looks solid but hides the crumbling beneath.

parallels.desc: you shall do no injustice in court

verseByVerse.quote: "And Paul said, 'I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest, for it is written, "You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Paul said, “I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest, for it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’”

I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest. Key words. How could Paul not know? Perhaps poor eyesight (Galatians 4:15; 6:11); perhaps the high priest wasn’t in his robes at an informal meeting called by a Roman; perhaps Paul had been away for years. Or perhaps irony: I didn’t recognise a man acting like that as God’s high priest. The plain reading is a genuine apology.

For it is written, “You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.” From Exodus 22:28. Paul submits at once to Scripture. A model: when shown you are wrong by God’s word, yield.

In a sentence. Paul answered that he hadn’t realised he was the high priest, for Scripture says not to speak evil of a ruler of your people.

On a Tuesday. Respect the office, even when the officeholder is unworthy. And when Scripture corrects you, yield quickly.

parallels.desc: nor curse a ruler of your people

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when Paul perceived that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council, 'Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial.' And when he had said this, a dissension arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was divided."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when Paul perceived that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial.” And when he had said this, a dissension arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was divided.

When Paul perceived that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees. The council was split between the two parties.

Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. True. Paul never stopped thinking of himself as a Jew who believed in the Messiah (26:5; Philippians 3:5).

It is with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial. Key words. Not a trick, but the heart of the matter. The real issue was the resurrection: Jesus had risen, which proves the resurrection of the dead. The hope of Israel (26:6–8; 28:20) is fulfilled in Christ’s resurrection.

A dissension arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was divided. Paul exposed their divisions, and the council fell apart.

In a sentence. Seeing that some were Sadducees and others Pharisees, Paul called out that he was a Pharisee, the son of Pharisees, on trial for the hope of the resurrection of the dead, and at this the Pharisees and Sadducees began to quarrel and the assembly split.

For worship. The resurrection is the hope of Israel and of the world. Hold on to it.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all. Then a great clamor arose, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees' party stood up and contended sharply, 'We find nothing wrong in this man. What if a spirit or an angel spoke to him?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all. Then a great clamor arose, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees’ party stood up and contended sharply, “We find nothing wrong in this man. What if a spirit or an angel spoke to him?”

For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all. The Sadducees, the priestly party, rejected the Pharisees’ oral traditions and doctrines not found clearly in the five books of Moses. Jesus answered them from Moses (Luke 20:27–38). The Pharisees believed in resurrection, angels and spirits.

We find nothing wrong in this man. Key words. Pharisees defending Paul. Party loyalty overcame their hostility.

What if a spirit or an angel spoke to him? They allowed that his Damascus experience might be genuine, though they wouldn’t say it was Jesus. An echo of Gamaliel (5:39).

In a sentence. The Sadducees say there is no resurrection, angels or spirits, but the Pharisees believe in all of them, so there was a great uproar, and some scribes of the Pharisees stood up and argued that they found nothing wrong with this man, and perhaps a spirit or angel had spoken to him.

On a Tuesday. Rejecting the supernatural leaves no room for the gospel. Christianity stands or falls with the resurrection.
verseByVerse.note: The Sadducees, the priestly party, rejected the Pharisees’ oral traditions and probably held the five books of Moses above the rest of Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the dissension became violent, the tribune, afraid that Paul would be torn to pieces by them, commanded the soldiers to go down and take him away from among them by force and bring him into the barracks."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the dissension became violent, the tribune, afraid that Paul would be torn to pieces by them, commanded the soldiers to go down and take him away from among them by force and bring him into the barracks.

The tribune, afraid that Paul would be torn to pieces by them. The highest court of Israel nearly tearing a man apart. The tribune was getting nowhere.

Commanded the soldiers to go down and take him away from among them by force and bring him into the barracks. Rescued a second time by Rome.

In a sentence. When the dispute turned violent, the commander, afraid Paul would be torn apart, ordered soldiers to take him from them by force and bring him back to the barracks.

For worship. God protected Paul again and again. He is faithful to his servants.

verseByVerse.quote: "The following night the Lord stood by him and said, 'Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome.' When it was day, the Jews made a plot and bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they had killed Paul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The following night the Lord stood by him and said, “Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome.” When it was day, the Jews made a plot and bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they had killed Paul.

The following night the Lord stood by him. Key words. Paul was probably discouraged: rejected by his people, nearly killed twice, his testimony in Jerusalem apparently a failure. And the Lord stood by him. Jesus himself (2 Timothy 4:17). The Lord stood by him in the dark, in the barracks.

Take courage. “Take courage” (tharsei): the word Jesus used to the paralysed man, the sick woman, the disciples in the storm (Matthew 9:2, 22; 14:27).

For as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome. Key words. Jesus calls his Jerusalem testimony a success: you have testified. Faithfulness, not results. And a promise: “must” (dei), you will get to Rome. Paul’s desire (19:21; Romans 1:10–11) will be fulfilled. This promise held him through two years in prison, shipwreck and snakebite.

When it was day, the Jews made a plot and bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they had killed Paul. A curse on themselves (anathematisan). A hunger strike for murder.

In a sentence. The next night the Lord stood by Paul and told him to take courage, for as he had testified about him in Jerusalem, he must testify also in Rome, and when day came the Jews formed a plot and swore not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul.

On a Tuesday. In your darkest night, the Lord stands by you. Take courage; his promises hold.

verseByVerse.quote: "There were more than forty who made this conspiracy. They went to the chief priests and elders and said, 'We have strictly bound ourselves by an oath to taste no food till we have killed Paul.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
There were more than forty who made this conspiracy. They went to the chief priests and elders and said, “We have strictly bound ourselves by an oath to taste no food till we have killed Paul.

There were more than forty who made this conspiracy. A serious threat. Forty against one.

They went to the chief priests and elders. Key words. Religious leaders agreeing to murder. The same men who plotted against Jesus. The rabbis allowed vows to be released if they became impossible to keep; presumably they didn’t starve.

In a sentence. More than forty men were in this plot, and they went to the chief priests and elders and told them they had sworn a solemn oath not to eat until they had killed Paul.

For worship. Forty men vowed to kill Paul; one promise from Christ kept him alive. Count God’s promises bigger than your threats.

parallels.desc: Saul’s rash oath

verseByVerse.quote: "'Now therefore you, along with the council, give notice to the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to determine his case more exactly. And we are ready to kill him before he comes near.' Now the son of Paul's sister heard of their ambush, so he went and entered the barracks and told Paul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now therefore you, along with the council, give notice to the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to determine his case more exactly. And we are ready to kill him before he comes near.” Now the son of Paul’s sister heard of their ambush, so he went and entered the barracks and told Paul.

Give notice to the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to determine his case more exactly. A trap, using a fake legal hearing.

And we are ready to kill him before he comes near. An ambush in the narrow streets between the fortress and the council chamber.

Now the son of Paul’s sister heard of their ambush. Key words. This is the only mention of Paul’s family in Jerusalem. We know nothing else about his sister or nephew. Perhaps his family hadn’t disowned him (Philippians 3:8). God used a boy who happened to overhear. Nothing happens by chance.

So he went and entered the barracks and told Paul. Brave: he risked the conspirators’ anger.

In a sentence. The plotters asked the council to request the commander to bring Paul down, pretending to examine his case more carefully, while they waited to kill him on the way, but Paul’s nephew heard of the ambush, went into the barracks and told Paul.

On a Tuesday. God uses ordinary people, even young ones, to fulfil his promises. Be ready to be used.
verseByVerse.note: This is the only mention of Paul’s family in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul called one of the centurions and said, 'Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to tell him.' So he took him and brought him to the tribune and said, 'Paul the prisoner called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, as he has something to say to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to tell him.” So he took him and brought him to the tribune and said, “Paul the prisoner called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, as he has something to say to you.”

Paul called one of the centurions. Key words. Paul trusts God’s promise, and uses ordinary means. Faith in God’s sovereignty doesn’t mean doing nothing. God promised Rome; Paul still acted wisely.

Paul the prisoner. Paul later called himself “a prisoner of Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 3:1; Philemon 1). Not Rome’s prisoner, but Christ’s.

In a sentence. Paul called a centurion and asked him to take the young man to the commander, since he had something to tell him, and the centurion did, saying Paul the prisoner had asked him to bring the young man.

For worship. Trusting God and acting wisely go together. Use the means he gives.

verseByVerse.quote: "The tribune took him by the hand and going aside asked him privately, 'What is it that you have to tell me?' And he said, 'The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though they were going to inquire somewhat more closely about him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tribune took him by the hand and going aside asked him privately, “What is it that you have to tell me?” And he said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though they were going to inquire somewhat more closely about him.

The tribune took him by the hand and going aside asked him privately. Key words. A kind, almost fatherly touch. The young man may have been a boy. The tribune handled it wisely and discreetly.

The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow. He tells the plan.

In a sentence. The commander took him by the hand, drew him aside and asked privately what he had to say, and he said the Jews had agreed to ask him to bring Paul before the council tomorrow, pretending to look into his case more carefully.

On a Tuesday. Kindness from unexpected people is God’s grace too. Thank him for it.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him, who have bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they have killed him. And now they are ready, waiting for your consent.' So the tribune dismissed the young man, charging him, 'Tell no one that you have informed me of these things.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him, who have bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they have killed him. And now they are ready, waiting for your consent.” So the tribune dismissed the young man, charging him, “Tell no one that you have informed me of these things.”

But do not be persuaded by them. Bold advice from a young man to a Roman officer.

And now they are ready, waiting for your consent. Urgent: it was planned for tomorrow.

Tell no one that you have informed me of these things. Protecting the boy, and the secret.

In a sentence. He urged the commander not to agree, since more than forty men were waiting in ambush, sworn not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul, and were ready, awaiting his consent, and the commander sent him away, telling him not to tell anyone he had reported this.

For worship. Plots against God’s people often fail through small, hidden means. God is never outwitted.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The commander calls two centurions and orders two hundred soldiers, seventy cavalry and two hundred spearmen to be ready to leave for Caesarea at nine that night, with horses for Paul, to bring him safely to Governor Felix. He writes a letter: Claudius Lysias greets His Excellency Felix. The Jews had seized this man and were about to kill him when he rescued him with his troops, having learned he was a Roman. Wanting to know the charge, he brought him before their council and found it concerned disputes about their law, nothing deserving death or prison. Told of a plot against the man, he has sent him at once and instructed his accusers to bring their case to Felix. The soldiers take Paul overnight as far as Antipatris; next day the cavalry go on with him while the rest return. In Caesarea they deliver the letter and hand Paul over. Felix reads it, asks his province, and on hearing Cilicia says he will hear the case when the accusers arrive. He orders Paul kept under guard in Herod’s palace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Providence Wearing a Uniform

Nothing in this section is miraculous, and that is the theological point. The God who opened the Philippian jail with an earthquake here uses a boy's ears, an officer's fear of a court-martial, a standard troop deployment, and a piece of self-serving correspondence. Scripture is entirely comfortable with both, and Christians who will only recognise God's hand in the spectacular will miss most of what he does.

Two guards keep this from turning into fatalism. First, providence does not excuse the wickedness it employs: the chief priests who agreed to supply the pretext for a murder are guilty of it, and Lysias's falsified report is a lie, and Luke's silence is not approval. Second, providence does not promise comfort. This chapter's happy ending is a two-year detention under a governor angling for a bribe. God's certain purposes and a believer's real losses run down the same road, at the same time, and Scripture never asks anyone to pretend otherwise.

The pattern is Joseph's: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Gen. 50:20). The forty men were, without knowing it, working for the One they were trying to thwart — and so was the empire, which spent a great deal of money that night keeping alive a man it would one day execute.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The tribune's letter told the governor a true story arranged to flatter its author. He did not invent a single fact. He moved one clause — putting the discovery of Paul's citizenship before the rescue instead of after it — and let his superior draw a generous conclusion. Luke set the letter down beside the events of the previous chapter and left it there.

Now: Take the story you tell most often about a hard episode — why the job ended, why the friendship cooled, how the argument went. You have told it enough times that it runs smoothly now. Every detail in it probably happened. Then lay it beside a transcript, the way Luke lays this letter beside chapter 22, and ask the narrower question: is the sequence right, and is the motive you imply the motive you actually had? Most of us are not liars. Most of us are editors, and the edit is nearly always in our own favour.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then he called two of the centurions and said, 'Get ready two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to go as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night. Also provide mounts for Paul to ride and bring him safely to Felix the governor.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he called two of the centurions and said, “Get ready two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to go as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night. Also provide mounts for Paul to ride and bring him safely to Felix the governor.”

Get ready two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen. Key words. 470 soldiers to protect one prisoner from forty assassins. Nearly half the Jerusalem garrison. Rome took the protection of a citizen seriously, and the tribune wasn’t taking chances. God’s promise kept Paul; Rome supplied the escort.

To go as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night. The ESV notes that the third hour of the night was about 9 p.m. Under cover of darkness.

Also provide mounts for Paul to ride. More than one: perhaps for changes of horse, or for his companions.

And bring him safely to Felix the governor. Felix, governor of Judea about AD 52–59. A former slave, freed by the emperor’s family. The historian Tacitus said he exercised royal power with the mind of a slave.

In a sentence. Then he called two centurions and ordered them to prepare two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to leave for Caesarea at nine that night, and to provide horses for Paul and take him safely to Governor Felix.

On a Tuesday. God sent 470 soldiers to escort one apostle. He can protect you too.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the third hour of the night was about 9 p.m. Felix, a former slave, was governor of Judea from about AD 52 to 59.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he wrote a letter to this effect: 'Claudius Lysias, to his Excellency the governor Felix, greetings.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he wrote a letter to this effect: “Claudius Lysias, to his Excellency the governor Felix, greetings.

And he wrote a letter to this effect. “To this effect”: Luke gives the substance, perhaps from a copy read at the trial.

Claudius Lysias. Claudius Lysias probably took the emperor’s name when he bought his citizenship (22:28). Lysias was his Greek name.

To his Excellency the governor Felix. “Excellency” (kratistō): the same title Luke uses for Theophilus (Luke 1:3). A formal Roman letter.

In a sentence. He wrote a letter: Claudius Lysias to His Excellency Governor Felix, greetings.

For worship. God’s plans unfold even through official letters and bureaucracy. He is Lord of the paperwork too.
verseByVerse.note: Claudius Lysias probably took the emperor’s name when he bought his citizenship.

parallels.desc: “most excellent”

verseByVerse.quote: "'This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen.

This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the soldiers and rescued him. True.

Having learned that he was a Roman citizen. Key words. Lysias leaves out that he had nearly flogged a Roman citizen, and implies he rescued Paul because he was a citizen. In fact he only learned it later (22:25–29). A small, self-serving twist of the facts. Luke, the careful historian, preserves both versions honestly.

In a sentence. He wrote that this man had been seized by the Jews and was about to be killed when he came with soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen.

On a Tuesday. It’s tempting to tell the story so we look good. Tell the truth, even when it’s unflattering.
verseByVerse.note: Lysias leaves out that he had nearly flogged a Roman citizen.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And desiring to know the charge for which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council. I found that he was being accused about questions of their law, but charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And desiring to know the charge for which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council. I found that he was being accused about questions of their law, but charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment.

I found that he was being accused about questions of their law. Religious disputes, as Gallio said (18:15).

But charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment. Key words. A Roman official declares Paul innocent. Luke records such verdicts repeatedly (25:25; 26:31–32): Paul, like Jesus, was innocent under Roman law. Important for Theophilus, and for the church’s standing in the empire.

In a sentence. Wanting to know the charge, he brought him before their council and found that the accusation concerned questions of their law, with no charge deserving death or imprisonment.

For worship. Christians should live so that even unbelieving authorities find no fault in them (1 Peter 2:12).

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him.

When it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once. Passing the problem upwards.

Ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him. A proper Roman trial would follow.

In a sentence. When he learned of a plot against the man, he sent him at once to Felix, and ordered his accusers to present their case before him.

On a Tuesday. God uses governments to provide due process. Pray for just courts.

verseByVerse.quote: "So the soldiers, according to their instructions, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris. And on the next day they returned to the barracks, letting the horsemen go on with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the soldiers, according to their instructions, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris. And on the next day they returned to the barracks, letting the horsemen go on with him.

Brought him by night to Antipatris. Antipatris was about 35 miles from Jerusalem; the road beyond ran through open, mostly Gentile country, safer from ambush. A forced march through the night.

And on the next day they returned to the barracks, letting the horsemen go on with him. The foot soldiers went back; the cavalry took him the last 25 miles.

In a sentence. The soldiers followed orders, took Paul by night to Antipatris, and the next day returned to the barracks, leaving the cavalry to go on with him.

For worship. God’s escort brought Paul safely through the night. He brings his people through every dark road.
verseByVerse.note: Antipatris was about 35 miles from Jerusalem; the road beyond was safer, running through mostly Gentile country.
